Mr. CASGRAIN-by Mr. Clarke-asked :
1.	Has one Doctor Ellis been employed by the government as port physician, or medical examiner of immigrants landing at Quebec, during the years 1902 and 1903, or during either of each years ?
2.	Is the said Doctor Ellis employed by the government in any other capacity in connection with the medical service in and about the port of Quebec ? If so, what are his duties ?
3.	Has the said Doctor Ellis an annual salary; or is he paid so much for the season, or in any other way ?
4.	What is the amount of the remuneration, either annual or otherwise, of the said Doctor Ellis ?
5.	Is Doctor Howe employed by the government as port physician at Quebec, or medical examiner of immigrants, or in some other capacity In and about the said port ; and in what capacity ?
6.	What is the salary or remuneration of the said Doctor Howe ?

In the absence of the minister, I beg to reply as follows :
1.	Dr. Ellis was employed for about two or three weeks of the year 1903, in supervising the examination of immigrants landing at Quebec, under the new regulations which had just come into force at that port.
2.	Dr. Ellis is the medical officer of the Department of the Interior, and subject to the direction of the department as to his services. He is also the medical examiner at St. John, his headquarters being at that port.
3.	Dr. Ellis is not employed by the season, but by salary.
4.	The salary paid to Dr. Ellis is at the rate of $2,000 per annum, his whole time being engaged by the department.
5.	There are two medical attendants in connection with the immigration service at Quebec. Dr. Arthur Potvin is the medical attendant on all patients in the immigration hall, or those who may he compelled to remain over for hospital or other treatment, having been rejected or refused permission to go forward to destination until they are cured of the diseases for which they were rejected. Dr. Howe is medical examiner of immigrants at the same port.
6.	Dr. Howe is paid by fees and receives $5 for every vessel examined by him with 100 immigrant passengers or less, and ten cents extra per head for every immigrant passenger over 100, provided his total earnings do not exceed $100 in any one month. If the fees exceed the amount named his total allowance is $100.

speechtext:
House again in committee on Bill (No. 21) to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways.-The Minister of Railways and Canals.
On section 3,

The minister informed us, when last we were considering this Bill, that he would consider whether the Bill should be made to apply to express companies or not. What has been tbe result of his consideration in this respect ?

I have been considering the matter carefully since the last sitting of the committee, and I have come to the conclusion that, considering the enormous magnitude of the Bill, it would be quite impracticable to encumber it with any further provisions if it is to be disposed of during the present session. My own view is that if it is desirable express companies should be taken under control of tbe railway commission, it would be necessary to have that dealt with by a separate Bill. I cannot think of incorporating it in the present Bill. It would complicate it, and would involve a great deal of labour in making alterations and amendments in other clauses.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: Seeing that the minister has made a study of this matter, I would ask him whether the Inter-State Commerce Bill, and the several State Bills dealing with this matter, do not give jurisdiction over express companies ?

Except so far as they may con-

trol common carriers, I do not think that they deal with any of the express companies in any of the states.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is not an express company a common carrier ?
We are not dealing with the liability or the power of common carriers in this Bill ; we are dealing with railway carriers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The board of trade of the city of Toronto and other boards of trade have represented to the minister that it is essential the rates charged by express companies should be subject to regulation by the railway commission. I agree thoroughly with that idea. If this Bill is as comprehensive as it is said to be, it should contain such a provision, and without such a provision it is an incomplete Bill and almost useless. The express companies handle a great deal more freight now than ever before, and their charges in some cases are said to be excessive. The commercial people of this country desire that express companies should be included in this Bill, and I cannot see any reason why the minister purposes not to do so. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway have three or four car loads of express matter on each train now, whereas formerly half a car was sufficient for the express business. Again, it is the railway companies that own these express companies. As a matter of fact, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway own their express business. I again ask that the express companies be brought within the purview of this Bill.

I think the minister would do well to reconsider his intention not to include the express companies in this Bill. A few weeks ago the fruit-growers waited upon the minister and complained that their fruit, which is largely shipped by express, was subject to the discriminations and irregularities which this Bill is supposed to overcome in respect to railways. Hundreds of car loads of fruit are shipped by express, and it seems to me a reasonable thing that the express rates should be regulated by the railway commission. Not only the fruitgrowers, but other shippers are very anxious to have some regulation of express companies, and I trust the minister will include them in this Bill.
Mr. MeCREARY. I do not know why these hon. gentlemen bring up such matters as these at the present time, unless it be their object to defeat this Bill. While the express charges are very high throughout Canada, yet I believe that if we are going to hamper this Bill with every detail of transportation that can be thought of, the result will be to prevent its passage during the present session. I believe the majority of the members of this House are in favour of Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
having this Bill passed at once, and having the railway problem solved so far as it is possible to solve it in this respect.

Hear, hear.
Mr. MeCREARY. We cannot expect to cure every ill by one Act. This is something like the Municipal Act, and it will require amendments probably for the next four or five sessions before it is made nearly perfect. The railway Bills in Minnesota and Dakota have taken ten or twelve years since their passage to reach their present condition, and they are not perfect yet. We cannot expect to have this Bill perfect all at once, and if we desire to pass it this session we should not encumber it with details in regard to express charges or telephone charges or telegraph charges, or anything else but construction, equipment, management, operation and rates on railways. We could deal with the express companies either in a separate Bill or after we have finished the main body of this Bill.

So far as my knowledge goes of the agitation which was the cause of the introduction of the amendment to the Railway Act by the Minister of Railways and Canals, the complaint was in regard to freight tolls, and not, as the hon. gentleman seems to think, in regard to the construction of railways. The great complaint throughout this country was that the railways were not held within reasonable bounds in respect to freight rates, and express rates as well. If we are going to have a Bill dealing with the tolls on railways, why not have it regulate rates by express as well as by slow freight ?

I resent what the hon. gentleman from the west says. I am very anxious to see a railway commission Bill carried through the House, and I will do my best to help to get it passed. I believe the country will support the minister in putting such a Bill through but the country expects that a Bill dealing with freight rates will deal with all freight rates, including those of express companies. Why should not the railways be regulated in regard to the rates they charge on express matter as well as in regard to other freight ? Goods are sent by express not only for speed, but often also because they are perishable. Carload after carload of perishable freight is sent by express from the fruit districts of Ontario, and the fruit-growers have said time after time that they can only grow fruit under the condition of having favourable freight charges. If the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher)-and I would like to see him in his place to-day-wishes to aid the farmers, the fruit-growers and the dairymen of this country, he will see that this Bill takes jurisdiction over express charges, I am anxious to see the Bill passed, and I suggest to the minister now that there is no reason why he should not put into this

clause the word express or introduce later a clause, providing that express companies shall be considered railway companies, to make them subject to the jurisdiction of the Bill.

I am afraid that the jaunty way in which my hon. friend would dispose of the question and the confident ease witli which he thinks this matter can be dealt with, show that he has a lot to learn as to the proper and effective method of legislating on this question. The assumption of my hon. friend that we are withdrawing express companies for the carriage of goods from the operation of this Bill is a mistaken one. All arrangements between railway companies and express companies are subject to the control of this proposed legislation, and I do not myself apprehend that there will be a great deal of difficulty in a general or broad way in covering all reasonable complaints with regard to the carriage, not of express freight, but of express packages-all goods which are taken up by express companies. But beyond that it would be absolutely necessary, I may tell my hon. friend, in order that proper legislation on that subject should be on the statute-book, that it should be dealt with by itself in a separate Bill. I have given a great deal of attention to this and other questions in connection with the proposed Bill, and have spent a good deal of labour upon it, and I want to say to the hon. gentleman that what he suggests cannot be done. It would simply destroy the Bill, and probably would not be effective at all. But what my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) said a moment ago has much force in it. We cannot hope to exhaust all legislation for the carriage of merchandise by railways and other carriers in this Bill. I feel myself that we have undertaken as much as we can well and properly carry out during the present session. I do not want the Bill to be encumbered, if I can avoid it, with any new propositions. I want to deal with what we have here, and when we get this Bill in proper shape and working order, we shall have a footing on which to proceed to take up other cognate questions and deal with them in a much more effective manner than we could undertake to do in the present circumstances. Referring to what has been said by the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), I do recall that some delegations of fruit men waited upon me. but 1 do not know that they made any special reference to grievances which they suffered from the express companies. What they did impress on my mind was that, owing to the facility with which the railway companies were able to change their freight classifications, so as to transfer merchandise from one class to another, it was possible for them to do a good deal of injury to fruit and other perishable goods.
It was express freight, so far as my recollection serves me, that they had in mind, and as to which they impressed on me the need of improvement. We are covering express operations in a much larger degree, I believe, than the hon. gentleman imagines, because the word express company is not in the Bill. A railway company cannot, through an express company or other instrumentality, exact exorbitant charges. Its actions over its line are controlled by this board. I do not know how much more you could ask in a general way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Suppose the railway company were an express company, could it not evade the law ?

I do not think it could if. it were an express company any more than it could if it were not. I do not think, as legal entities, any of the railway companies are express companies. I suppose some of the individuals who constitute one company may constitute the other ; but for all legal purposes they are distinct corporate bodies. I believe that to be the case in regard to the Canadian Pacific Express Company, and I think it is likely to be the case with regard to the others. If my hon. friend desires, as I believe he does, to see this legislation go through, he will not urge that it should be encumbered with an attempt to deal with other questions than those included in it, and I would strongly counsel him to have patience with regard to these matters which he has in his mind, because in another session somebody will be able to take them up and deal' with them if we are not here to do it. We certainly have a very large contract on our hands to get through with ail these various clauses, and discuss all the complicated questions involved in the Bill, without increasing the number.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This Bill proposes to give to the commissioners the absolute power to fix rates.
We have not come to that yet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
We are discussing it under this clause. I do not see how it would encumber the Bill or affect it in the slightest to give these commissioners power to deal with rates on freight carried either as express freight or in any other manner by a railway. Express companies are put to much more expense handling small freights in the different sections of the country than railway companies are subjected to on the average class of freights they carry. But the commission could make allowance for the difference and could fix the rates accordingly. And inasmuch as the express companies deal with nearly every individual in the community, inasmuch as, compared with railway companies! they stand pretty much in the position of re-

tailers as compared with wholesale dealers,
X fail to see why the commission should not have the power of fixing express rates as well as rates on ordinary freight. In the American states, jurisdiction is given the commissioners to deal with this very class of freight. Then, it is provided that this Act shall apply to all persons, companies and railways other than government railways, within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada. I suppose the hon. Minister of Railways knows what particular railways are not within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada. I believe that all railways with a provincial charter, concerning which there is no express enactment declaring them to be works for the general advantage of Canada, and some railways which have a special charter subjecting their rates to the approval of the Governor General in Council, would be removed from the jurisdiction of this commission. X would ask the hon. minister what railways are included or excluded.

There is no doubt that a portion of the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway would not come under this commission, so far as any reduction in their rates is concerned, unless their income should come up to a certain percentage.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How much of the main line ?
From Callander west.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is nearly the whole railway.

They have a good many more miles of railway in the west of Canada subject to this commission than would not come under it. They are extending lines in all possible directions. Their whole system in the east of Canada would come under the operation of this Bill. Year by year the mileage of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which would be subject entirely to the control of the railway commission as regards rates, will be increasing. My hon. friend is under the impression that none of those railways should come within the operation of this Bill which were incorporated under the old Railway Act, and allowed a margin of 15 per cent. I think that the hon. gentleman is in error. I have no doubt, and I think that legal opinion will bear me out, that there are no other companies incorporated in Canada which would be exempt except that portion of the Canadian Pacific Railway I have named. It is perhaps true that railways with local charters and which have not come under the legislative jurisdiction of the federal parliament would be exempt from the operation of the Act. But there are very few Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
lines of any importance, and their mileage is very limited indeed, which have not been brought within the jurisdiction of this parliament. But if it should become necessary, by reason of the amount of business done, or because of any complaints concerning rates, that parliament should have authority,
there is a very easy and simple method of obtaining that control. A general Act declaring these roads to be works for the general advantage of Canada would bring them within the jurisdiction of this House. On the whole, I think that railways doing 95 per cent of the business of Canada will come within this section.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister, in reply to a statement of mine, says that this Bill will apply to certain railways which were chartered at a particular time when the Railway Act provided that there ' would be no interference with the rates until they had earned at least 15 per cent on their capital. But what I pointed out was that this provision operated in the nature of a contract between the government and these companies. I understand that the power is vested in this government of absolutely expropriating without remuneration at all to these railways. But they got their charters when the general Railway Act provided that there would be no interference with the rates until they had earned 15 per cent. It is true, we have the power, but will it not be an interference with the mutual contract or understanding applicable to every railway company which received a charter under that particular Railway Aet ? Though you may have the power, the moral obligation, the mutual contract remains with these railway companies, which got their charters at that particular time. Then, as to the application, the hon. minister admits that these roads which are not under the jurisdiction of Canada by being declared works for the benefit of Canada would not be subject to this commission.
As regards control over the rates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I suppose the hon. minister does not argue that the commission would have power to regulate rates on roads which are purely provincial and have not been brought under the jurisdiction of this parliament by the clause declaring them to be of general advantage to Canada.
I would like to see a decision on that question-whether the general Act of the Dominion which states that all railways which touch or cross government railways, the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway, are brought under the jurisdiction of Canada, is valid. It is possible it may be so, but I doubt the legality of it. To bring a work under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada you should at least specifically declare what work it is.

In the case of a railway you should name the two points between which you assume jurisdiction over that railway. If my interpretation of the law in that respect is correct, the jurisdiction which we can confer upon this commission will be a very limited one. It will cover works which receive their entity from the Dominion parliament, except as the hon. minister says, the Canadian Pacific Railway from Callander westward ; but it will not cover roads which have provincial charters. Morally, if not legally, it must exclude roads which receive their charter under the virtual notice given by the government that the parties investing money in railway enterprises need dread no fear of interference with rates until they have declared a dividend of fifteen per cent. I doubt very much that it can apply to those roads which were supposed to be brought under the jurisdiction of the Dominion parliament by being declared works for the general advantage of Canada, because they touch or cross the Intercolonial Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway. As I say if we have power to take over the jurisdiction over these roads, it should be by a specific declaration as to the points between which our jurisdiction is to extend. If my contention is correct, this Bill will have an application only to a moiety, perhaps to a minority, of the railways in the Dominion.

I must confess that I am quite unable to form an opinion as to what is the attitude of the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) on this question-his mental attitude or his political attitude. He attacks this Bill because of its limited application. The apparent inference is that it is not worth while to promote a Bill looking to the establishment of a railway commission because of this limited application, and I understand, for that reason he opposes the Bill. Is that his attitude ? Is it possible that he opposes the Bill on the ground that it is not more comprehensive, while he argues that it cannot be made more comprehensive? Is that his attitude ? My hon. friend, then, I assume, is in that frame of mind. But, how comes this, when he was such a red-hot, enthusiastic supporter of a railway commission not nearly so far reachng in its power as this, which his friend the late Mr. Dalton McCarthy tried to establish by the measure which he introduced session after session in this House. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) ardently supported that Bill and was deeply pained that it did not receive the support he thought its merits justified. What is the difference between the conditions then and the conditions now ? The same special contract was in existence and confirmed by legislation with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and that company covered a larger proportion of the territory under which railways within our jurisdiction were huilt than it does to-day. The
same law existed then which exists to-day with regard to the power of the provincial legislatures and our legal attitude towards local roads was exactly the same. Why is it that when the difficulties were much more serious than they are to-day my hon. friend so warmly supported the Bill which he cannot support to-day ? Now, lie says that in this Bill there is an element that is immoral
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Immoral ?

Yes, immoral. The hon. gentleman says it may be legal, but it would be immoral for this parliament to take away from the companies which were incorporated under the former Railway Act, the privilege of exemption from control of rates until the time when their profits realized fifteen per cent. It may be legal, he says, but it is wrong. Now, by whom was the wrong done ? By my hon. friend himself. How is it possible for me to understand my hon. friend when he criticises a Bill which in this respect is simply a transcript of the Bill introduced by himself- or, if not by himself by the government of which he was a member-which gave control of these railways to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council irrespective of whether they were earning fifteen per cent or not. How is it that he can have got himself into such a frame of mind ? How can he so shut his memory against what he himself has done ? Is it any wonder that I find it difficult to understand what he his aiming at ? Is he for or against this measure ? If against it, is he against it for the reasons which existed when he was in favour of this class of legislation ? If I do him less than the justice he may think he is entitled to, it is only because I am unable to comprehend the position in which he stands.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals cannot mention anything I have ever said against the creation of a tribunal for the purpose of controlling railways. I was not arguing in that light at all, the hon. minister must notice it. I was pointing out that this Bill had application to only a moiety of the railways of the Dominion, as against the claim of the hon. minister that it had application to nearly the whole of them. I was pointing out that it could have no application to provincial railways. I pointed out-and the Minister of Railways and Canals admitted that point-that it had no application to that portion of the Canadian Pacific Railway west of Callander. I expressed doubt of its applicability to those roads which were supposed to have been brought under our jurisdiction by the section of the law which declares them works for the general advantage of Canada. But all this is no reason why I should object to the Bill itself. I was a party to the Act-

at least I was supporting tlie government under which the law was passed-which virtually gave notice to every man who invested in a Canadian railway that there would be no interference with railway rates until fifteen per cent profit had been paid. I was also a party to the Bill which annulled that, and which would make it exclude from the benefits of that section all the roads which received their charters afterwards. Does that mean that I changed my mind as to the application of that section while it was in force ? Not at all. 1 am simply pointing out that this Bill would have application to comparatively few of the roads in Canada. The hon. gentleman refers to my attitude in the past

Does the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) say that under the Railway Act introduced by the government of which he was a member and which is in force today, that railways incorporated prior to a certain date were exempted from the operation of the Act ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not say anything of the kind. What I stated was that the moment that law was passed, it was a notice to every one who got a charter under it that there were no conditions in it such as that under the fifteen per cent clause. That does not say that because the Act was passed that from that time any person applying for a charter had a different notice-
It does distinctly and absolutely.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It does ?
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I say not. That is my opinion to-day. Why, then, can you not take under control the Canadian Pacific Railway Company ?

The hon. gentleman asks me a question, I will tell him. Because there was a distinct contract between the government of Canada and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and that contract was confirmed by this parliament; and we could not, we would not, no man would venture, without the sanction of the Railway Committee under these circumstances, to rescind that contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That contract is no more binding than a contract made with any other company under the general Railway Act, in which rates are not to be interfered with until they earn fifteen per cent. You changed that law, and you took away from them some rights which were virtually a contract with these companies. You have the same power to take jurisdiction over the Canadian Pacific Railway. No contract should interfere with such control if it is Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
necessary in the interest of the public. The hon. minister knows that he can take the Canadian Pacific Railway Company under control, notwithstanding the contract that the government made with them, and put them under the jurisdiction of this Act, the same as he can any other railway, the same as he can when he assumes jurisdiction over a provincial railway by claiming it to be for the general advantage of Canada. In the same way he could declare this work to be for the general advantages of Canada, notwithstanding the conditions of the contract and the part of the charter they may have received from a provincial government. By the terms of his commission, in proposing to take control of the railways he violates contracts, he violates solemn agreements embodied in the statute-book, just as much as he would by taking control over the rates of the Canadian Pacific Railway and putting them under the control of this commission. I am not arguing against the commission, I am merely pointing out the anomalies and the troubles the minister has to get over, and when I do so he should not attack my inconsistency for supporting the Bill establishing a railway commission introduced by the late Mr. McCarthy some years ago. I am of the same opinion still; but even if I had altered my opinions or discarded them, that is no reason why the hon. gentleman should complain. During my lifetime I have discarded or altered many opinions which I formerly held, and if they are of any advantage to the hon. gentleman he is welcome to them. I would say with the late hon. Mr. Howe, that no man has more contempt than I have for opinions which I have altered or discarded in my lifetime.
The minister has referred to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company as being, in a way, outside the jurisdiction of this Act.
No, I said in one respect only, and that is the control of rates. In every other respect the company is entirely under our control.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I am coming to that point. There is already a way to bring the Canadian Pacific Railway and its rates under the jurisdiction of this parliament and of this commission, and it is set out in the contract which he has quoted, and I have myself referred to many times in this House. The clause which regulates the charge's of the Canadian Pacific Railway is this :
20. The limit to the reduction of tolls by the parliament of Canada provided for by the eleventh subsection of the 17th section of the * Consolidated Railway Act, 1879,' respecting tolls, is hereby extended so that such reduction may be to such an extent that such tolls when reduced shall not produce less than ten per cent per annum profit on the capital act-

ually expended in the construction of the railway.
Now, we have asked this government to ascertain in some way what the actual cost of the Canadian Pacific Itailway was, as set out in this Act, and the government have never done so. But the moment it is done the Canadian Pacific Railway and all its charges can be brought under our control. I believe that time has arrived now. They are earning sufficient on the actual expenditure incurred to bring them within the jurisdiction of the Act, and one reason why we need this railway commission is to ascertain what the actual cost of the Canadian Pacific Railway has been as provided in this Act. I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) in regard to the partial jurisdiction of parliament over these railways. I believe this parliament has an absolute and supreme jurisdiction over these railways. If we have not supremacy, we ought to have it. I do not believe that we are bound so much by the vested rights of the companies, because the whole tenor of our parliamentary institutions is to take jurisdiction over these railways and to regulate them in the public interest, no matter what the past legislation may have been, and I believe no injustice would be done to the shareholders, the stockholders or any one else, and it is high time that parliament should take possession. The Minister of Justice, although he has heretofore strongly argued for vested interests, I am glad to see now that, by giving his consent to this Bill, he abandons somewhat his former position, and that it is now the intention of the government to take complete jurisdiction over all these railways. This parliament has now jurisdiction over all the other railways, and the only one excluded, the Canadian Pacific Railway, can be brought under by this commission immediately if the government should take the steps providing for it in the Act incorporating the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Now, to return to the question of the express companies. The minister says that he does not wish to encumber the Bill. Does he not see that if he allows the express companies to remain outside he gives the railway companies an opportunity of evading the Bill ? They will turn themselves into express companies, and probably do all then-business as such, and in that way they will get outside the jurisdiction of the Bill. The way to regulate the whole of them is to bring them under the jurisdiction of this Act.

I wish to point out that it is very essential that we should include the express companies in this section three. Of course, as the Minister of Railways and Canals is aware, the express companies with which we have to deal are closely connected with the railway companies. They may be
separate legal entities, they are no doubt; but the connection is notorious. It is so close that undoubtedly if the railway commission for which this Bill provides secures any amelioration in the matter of rates, there will be a tendency in the railway companies to take back in the matter of express charges what has been lost in railway charges. I think that applies not only to the community in general, not only to fruit growers, but to that numerous class of persons who ship perishable goods of other kinds. I am sure that the advantage of the railway commission, if there is any, will be in many cases totally lost unless it has control over express rates. I point that out to the minister, because I feel convinced from my experience that there will be a tendency to take out of the public in express charges what may be lost by the commission taking control of the railroad rates. For my part I have very little faith myself in a commission. I believe in retaining in the hands of the minister all that authority which, to a certain extent, he is now divesting himself of in the creation of this commission. I believe in responsible control. I believe it is better for the department to have under its control a large number of experienced men of whom the minister himself should be the responsible head, and in all important matters he should be responsible to parliament. But that is outside the clause we are now discussing. This question of express charges, I do not think, will encumber the Bill. It will enable the commission to act equitably with these parties and it is absolutely essential for the proper and successful application of the Bill.

Mr. Chairman, I regret to hear the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals say that it is not possible to bring express companies under the provisions of this Bill. I hope he will find a way, on further consideration of the Bill, to bring express companies under its operation. The express and railway companies are intimately connected especially when we consider the relationship of the Canadian and Dominion express companies with. Canadian railway companies. If they are not the same as the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific Railway Companies they are at any rate owned and operated by the same men. We know as a matter of fact that if any complaint is made to the express companies in regard to the rates the onus is very frequently thrown on the railway companies, and the immediate reply is: We have to pay so much to the railway company that we are unable to reduce these rates. In some cases the payment has to be made by the express company to a railway company other than with which it is connected. I know of numerous cases where express companies have charged very much higher rates for carrying carloads of fruit a short distance than they have charged for
/

carrying them a much longer distance by their own company, and when asked why they should charge so much more for carrying fruit for a short distance than for a long distance, the reply was :	We have to
pass over another railway, we have to pay it a fixed charge, and having to pay that charge, we are unable to reduce the rates. The "express companies say positively, and apparently, candidly, that the charges they are making are not excessive, because they are not able to pay their shareholders more than 6 per cent dividend. We have no means of knowing whether this is true or not. The railway and express companies are so intimately connected with each other that it may be that the express companies do not make more than 6 per cent, but it may also be the fact that any profit over and above that is credited to the railway companies. So it seems to me that there is very great reason why the express companies should be brought under the operation of this Bill on account of their intimate connection with the railway companies, so that they would not be able to shift the responsibility upon the shoulders of the railway companies. I notice that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals said that he did not remember that the fruit growers had brought this matter to his attention, but I read in the ' Globe ' of the 12th February, some remarks by one of the delegates who waited upon the hon. minister which would seem to indicate that the question of express rates was discussed :
Mr. Bunting, president of the Ontario Fruit Growers' Association, said that in September last 2,500 baskets of peaches were shipped by express from the Niagara district to points east of Toronto, principally Montreal. The transportation companies received thirteen and a-half cents per basket, whereas the grower received only eight and three-quarter cents.
I remember that statement was made, but I did not understand that it referred to express companies. I understood that it referred to express charges by the railway company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I know what the rate is from the Niagara district to Montreal. The express rate is 13J cents per basket, so that Mr. Bunting, in referring to it, evidently referred to the express company's charge, because that was the express company's charge.
I did not take it in that way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Yes, that was the express company's charge. They charge 80 cents per 100 pounds. I should hope, therefore, that the hon. minister will find a way to bring the operations of the express companies under this Bill. The express companies do a large portion of the business in fruit. From the Niagara district I should say that not less than $200,-Mr. SMITH (Wentworth).
000 annually are taken out in express charges on the fruit carried from that district. Whether this is more than ought to be taken out of this district it is difficult for us to say. We know that in many cases by a reduction of rates the fruit growers would capture markets that are now controlled by fruit from the United States. We think the companies can afford to carry fruit at a lower rate, but being unable to know ourselves, we cannot press our claim on the express companies with as much force as we could if we had definite information on the subject. The great Northwest is supplied with fruit from California and from Ontario. It absorbs an enormous quantity of fruit, and the demand is constantly increasing. Our fruit is of such a perishable nature that we require the best accommodation possible. We do not receive that at the present time. Our express service is very inferior indeed. The 1'ruit has to go by way of Ottawa and Carleton Junction instead of going by North Bay, and the train service is inferior. The fruit is not carried on the best trains and an enormous trade is lost to Canada and is placed in the hands of the fruit growers of California simply because the express service is not as good as it ought to be. I hope the liqp. minister will find his way clear to bringing the express companies under the operation of the commission, so that it will be able to control the rates and see that the railway companies do not charge the express companies more than they ought to charge them for carrying fruit cars.

I see the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) in his place now. I think he was otherwise engaged, and did not hear the argument of the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith). The statement has been made repeatedly that the fruit growers cannot get into the markets unless they have the best possible express service. They cannot hold the market of the North-west Territories unless there is some regulation of the charges made by these express companies, and I cannot see now, after all that has been said in this House, why these companies should not be brought under the jurisdiction and control of this commission. What is the reason of this protection that seems to be given to telephone and express companies in Canada ? Their charges are exorbitant. They are rivals of the government. The government is carrying on a large business in what is known as the parcel post system. They have a much better parcel post system in Europe than we have in Canada. We in Canada want to have the same kind of a parcel post system that they have in Europe, and we have asked for it, but for some reason we cannot get it. I know the reason. It is because of the influence which the express companies are able to exercise. They are able to wield

a potent influence that enables them to escape public jurisdiction and control of rates. It is time that these companies were regulated. The government has gone to the country and said they would propose legislation that would regulate all railway charges, and they bring down a Bill that completely ignores the most important feature of these charges. Why is this peculiar protection afforded to telephone companies and express companies ? Why should express companies not be brought under the jurisdiction of this Bill ? Why should the hon. Minister of Agriculture not go to his colleague the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and say :	In the interest of the farming community, in the interest of the dairying community, in the interest of the fruit-growers I recommend you to include provisions in the Bill dealing with railway companies for the complete control of express charges.

In the report of the interview of the delegation that waited on the government on the 11th February, in regard to the charges on fruit to which the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith) referred, I find that this statement was made :
A very large proportion of the fruit grown in the Niagara district, Is necessarily shipped by express. Taking express and freight rates together, and averaging the season through, one-third of the price realized on thie Niagara fruit sold in Montreal is absorbed in the carrying charges imposed for hauling from Niagara to Montreal.
In view of the fact that such a large proportion of this fruit is taken by express the hon. minister will see that it is a very important matter. I wish, however, while I am on my feet, to refer to the question of the appointment of the commission. I am not prepared to make any statement as to the legal aspect of this question. I do not know what the moral or legal obligation of the people of Canada is in respect to what dividends the railway shall earn, but I understand that the Canadian Pacific Railway are entitled to earn a dividend of 10 per cent on certain portions of their mainline before their rates can be regulated. It is news to me that any moral or legal obligation rested on the people so far as the other railroads are concerned. I am one of those who would not seek to interfere with vested rights or to enter upon a campaign to con-fiscatei the rights of any corporation or private individual. At the same time most people admit that so far as the tolls and freight charges on railways are concerned, the railways have been free up to the present time to impose just about what conditions they like upon shippers. Whether the Railway Committee of the Privy Council could or could not interfere for the protection of the public, the fact remains that up to the present that body has not done so. I have not myself been an enthusiastic sup-112
porter of the idea of a railway commission, because I have feared that perhaps the constitution of that commission might be such that it would not accomplish the ends we seek. The fact remains that there is today no control over railways, that the public have suffered and are suffering, and that some way or other the railways have been able in the past to get the ear of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council or the officials. Let me give an illustration which I think will convince every hon. member of this House. I put a question on the Order paper as to whether a certain classification of freight which had been framed by the railways had been authorized by the Governor General in Council. The Railway Act clearly states that it is the duty of the Governor General in Council to authorize this freight classification before it is put into effect, and so far as I know all such other classifications have been authorized in the past. The Minister of Railways replied to my question that the last freight classification authorized was in November, 1899, to take effect in January, 1900, and that none had been authorized since. I hold in my hand a freight classification issued by the railways which has never been submitted for the approval of the Governor General in Council. It contains all kinds of regulations which are no doubt all right from a railway standpoint, but what is to become of the public if every private individual or every public corporation in Canada can make rules and regulations to suit himself or themselves. Here is apparently a flagrant violation of the Railway Act. This unauthorized classification came into effect the first of May, 1903, and every pound of freight from the Atlantic to the Pacific is now being shipped under it. Surely this this would prove that if the railway commission is properly constituted and if this Bill is of any use, it will be a benefit to the public. I do not oppose this Bill. I quite believe that the minister realizes as a great many people realize, that the time has come when something should be done. It is not the intention of any one in this House I am sure to take away from the railways any vested rights or just privileges which they enjoy, but I repeat that the public should have some means of being heard before a tribunal whether it be a railway commission or a re-organizedl Railway Committee of the Privy Council. I would like the minister to explain how it comes that this freight classification can be issued by the railways in absolute violation of the law 1

I have never expressed any very enthusiastic opinion as to the outcome of such legislation as we are now considering. I have always felt that the public were hoping for and anticipating greater results than the operation of such a law would justify. I therefore am quite in sympathy with



those who have expressed tlielr doubts In that direction. But there is no doubt whatever in my mind that the Railway Commission of 'the Privy Council, composed as it is of members of the cabinet who have multitudinous duties to perform, is not a tribunal to do effective work, and I do not know of anything that can take its place except a railway commission. That seems to have been the judgment of all English speaking communities who have had the same experience as we have had. The opinion seems to he settled that the appointment of a railway commission is the best remedy to adopt. There may possibly have been instances where, when a railway commission was once constituted having control of railways and rates, the law under which it was constituted has been repealed, but I know of no such instance. X do think that these commissions afford a great deal "of protection to the public, and the public soon realize that they reap some results, perhaps quite beneficial results, from their constitution, although they may not have come up to their expectations in practice.
My hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) has called attention to the fact that the railways have sent out a joint freight classification to take effect on the first of May, without having obtained the approval of the Governor General in Council. I do not know how it would be possible for the Department of Railways to prevent them doing that. I do not know what measure of criticism or blame should be attached to the Department of Railways because of that, but I do say that it was a high-handed proceeding on the part of the railways all the same.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Hear, hear.
Is there no penalty against the railways ?
We have provided one in this Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: None in the present law?

No. It was an indefensible act on the part of the railways, without a word of communication being sent to myself or to my deputy ,or to any of the officers of the department. I confess that until the subject was mentioned the other day, I had not heard that this freight classification had been issued. I don't think that the department is at fault. It would be at fault if, knowing that this classification had issued, it failed to take any action the law empowered it to take in order to have that classification recalled or rescinded. I am now having the matter reported to me as to what remedy we have in our hands. The railway commission, I think, will be in a very different position. It will be their exclusive duty to see that the law is not violated and to see that those who violate it are brought to book. Acts of that kind they will be
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: amply competent to deal with ; and they will, I think, assure the public against offence in the future. The hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) almost suggests to my mind the case of an individual who has been crying out for a long time for a railway commission ; then he gets it, and, after he gets it, he enters upon a close scrutiny of the Bill to see if there is some little point that might be put into it which is not there; and, after having made patient search, he finds at last that, broad and comprehensive as this Bill is, there is one thing that it does not comprehend-it does not give the commission power over all express companies ; and the moment my hon. friend discovers that, he begins to preach that this Bill is no good. That is the one thing he is particularly anxious to have in it; there is nothing else that measures in value to that feature ; and because that is not in the Bill, he is going to give it no particular show. The hon. gentleman is running away with the idea that express companies will be allowed to run riot under cover of the railways, in handling express business. That is not permissible under the Bill. If the hon. memi-ber had listened to what I said a while ago, he would have heard from me that this Bill assumes control of the railways, and the railways could not put freight in the hands of express companies, and allow them under the cover of the railway to make all sorts of extravagant demands. In regard to the tolls that are to be paid to a railway company by an express company out of its earnings, they will be subject to the control of the commission.
We do not control the rates of express companies ?

No ; and you cannot do it with this Bill without encumbering the Bill needlessly, without introducing into it, almost from the first to the last, exceptions and amendments to such an extent that I tell this committee frankly I am not prepared to undertake it at this time. I am not able to do so. It requires more thought and time and care than I can give to it. When I tell the hon. gentleman that, he has only another year to wait. We have lived through the past without much control, according to the hon. gentleman ; we have lived down to the year of grace 1903 ; . and one might suppose that we could continue to live in the same way for another year. Any one who feels keenly on this matter might introduce a Bill himself, and I am sure it would receive the consideration of parliament. Such a measure should not control simply those express companies which are operated on railways, and let every other express company run free of control. That would be unjust. It will not do to deal partially with the question ; it will have to be dealt with carefully ; and I am not prepared to take that question up at

this session of parliament. If my hon. friend will apply that bright, penetrating, astute intellect of his to the serious questions which we may deal with in this Bill, I am sure that his assistance will he most valuable, and I shall be glad to have it, because I know that he has a great deal of interest in these general questions which are of public importance. But let me give my hon. friend one little word of advice. Do not assume, because these questions are not being dealt with, that there must be some motive or influence or power operating upon one's mind to prevent him dealing with them. My hon. friend is not one whit clearer from influences of that character than the people whom he criticises, and it would be much better and fairer on his part to deal with questions on their merits.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
On almost every occasion when I bring up questions in this House, the hon. gentleman undertakes to lecture me. I have a right to express my views here without being lectured by him, and I have a right to criticise his conduct whenever it seems well for me to do so.
r
And I have a right to lecture you.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
When I look at the hon. gentleman's administration of the Railway Department of this country, what do I find? I find that this illegal classification has existed for years without his protesting against it. What is he there for ? What do we pay him for ? Why does he not bring these companies to time ? As a matter of fact, not one dollar of tolls can be collected by these companies without being approved by the Governor in Council. Yet there sit fifteen men who confess here to-day that this thing has taken place, and nothing has been done for the protection of the public. The hon. gentleman has lectured me in regard to this question of express companies. He says an opportunity shall be given to me to amend. I propose an amendment now. Mr. Chairman, 1 beg to move to amend the clause by inserting the words ' express companies ' after the words ' to all ' in the first line. The hon. gentleman says that the opportunity will be open to me to do something next session. I am sent here to do something this session. It is all very fine for the hon. gentleman to talk about imputing motives. Probably he is inviting this kind of thing today so that the Bill will not pass. He has promised it for this year, and when we propose to make it a good and complete Bill, he gets up and assumes a fatherly air and lectures everybody who ventures to criticise it. That lecture may be worth little or much. It has very little influence on me. In the interest of the public, of the commercial community, of the farmers, of the fruit growers, I propose that this Bill shall take jurisdiction forthwith, from the time of its 112*
passage, over express companies as well as railway companies. Express companies are another name for railway companies, to enable them to evade the control of the law. Why not bring them under the law now ? It only means that another schedule of rates shall come under the jurisdiction of the commission. I wish to see this commission created. I wish to see the measure pass this session. I will give every assistance I can to have it become law this session, and I hope that the minister will listen to suggestions made by gentlemen on this side of the House for the purpose of making the Bill as good and complete as we can, without delivering lectures to them.

I do not see why the hon. minister should complain of too minute an analysis by an hon. member as he has done in the case of my hon. friend from York (Mr. Maclean). It is our duty to scrutinize most carefully every section of the Bill in order to make it as perfect as possible. But what I rose more particularly to refer to is the fact that a good many railways will be outside the jurisdiction of this commission. We first exclude the government railways. I do not see why we should. If a railway commission is a good thing, it ought to be equally as good for the farmer in the maritime provinces as for the farmer in Ontario. It is quite conceivable that the government, in its management of the Intercolonial Railway, may discriminate unjustly against one shipper in favour of another. It would do no injustice to government or to the people to make this Bill apply to government railways. Then we exclude a large portion of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and also railways with provincial charters. Leaving these out, the Bill will apply to only a few railways at the best, and shippers will be confronted with the same difficulty as they were met with a few years ago before certain railways were declared for the general advantage of Canada when they had one-half of a railway a provincial road and the other half a Dominion road. Suppose a shipper in Ontario sends something to the seaboard. He first sends his freight over a provincial railway and then there is a dispute. He complains of being charged higher rates than somebody else. The company reply that the rate was a through rate and governed partly by local and partly by federal authorities. Under what law will the citizen prosecute to get his rights ? Will the commission deal with that question ?
Section 5 specially provides that this Bill shall apply.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It applies to companies which are within the legislative authority of Canada, but these provincial railways are not.
With respect to their traffic they are.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
But not local traffic. What I was going to point out is that if this commission is to be as useful as we hope it will, it can only be made so by working in conjunction with provincial commissioners on the plan of the interstate law in the United States. We have an equal right to include electric railways just as well as steam. The interpretation clause says :
The expression ' railway ' means a.ny railway which the company has power to construct or operate.
If my hon. friend will turn to page 29. section 118, subsection F, he will find that the Act applies to electric railways.
I looked to the interpretation clause, assuming that the electric railways would be found there.
Can the hon. gentleman name any railways in the province of Ontario which are not subject to the control of this parliament ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is the Brockville and Westport.
That has a Dominion charter.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would the railway being built by the provincial government towards Temiscaming come under this ?

The number of railways which will not come under this commission is so small and their mileage so limited, that they are not worth considering. The Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway are the two great systems doing business in the older provinces and they apparently are going to do the business in tiie west.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Take Manitoba and Ontario, and the hon. gentleman will find there are quite a few.
The number is rapidly diminishing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But it seems to me if we want to make the best use of the Bill, we should have provincial commissions as well.
My hon. friend will find that all these railways will come under this Bill.
May be in the future, but not now. Will the hon. minister tell me why the government railway should not be under this commission ?

Why should it be ? Is there Mr. SPROULE.
any institution in the country more amenable to public opinion and to the demands which the public make, or one more likely to be run in the general interest than is the government railway ? You institute a commission practically free from control, but the management of a government railway would be infinitely more responsive to the demands of public opinion. That management can be got at, it can be got at here on the floor of parliament. That is why the Intercolonial Railway was expressly exempted from the Railway Act when it was first passed and why it has been exempted on the different occasions when the railway law has been revised or codified. There is no reason why the people should seek to control this road indirectly through a commission when they control it directly already.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I can only say I have heard a great many complaints of the management of the Intercolonial Railway and the discriminations it charges on freight carried over it.

You will hear a great many complaints. We have had many complaints, for instance, because we could not furnish cars during the great pressure of business. But that is not the fault of the road, and it is not a difficulty which the commission could solve. In response to the complaints which have been made parliament has been asked to furnish money to provide more cars, so as to make up the deficiency as rapidly as possible. The Intercolonial in this respect, is much more responsive to public opinion than an ordinary railway would be.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The complaints I speak of have gone much further than that, I have heard it claimed that the Intercolonial Railway would carry one man's goods, even, for instance, one man's furniture, for little or nothing, while it would charge another man the full rate. I have heard that freely stated.

I can only say to the hon. gentleman :	Do not believe these stories that
are circulated; they are pure gossip-nothing in them. There is no railway in the country that is not more likely to be influenced in the direction of discrimination than a government railway. A government railway cannot discriminate, for the management knows that what it does for one man it must do for another. No management could exist that would countenance or tolerate discrimination in any way; it would be heaping up untold trouble for itself. There was never such a thing known. It may be that, by the action of the Governor in Council, in the case of a great fire, or as a means of helping the sufferers from some other calamity, certain freight might be carried cheaply or for nothing. But as for

carrying one man's furniture for nothing while making others pay, under ordinary circumstances, nothing of the kind could occur; it is perfectly out of the bounds of possibility.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would like to rest in the conclusion that the hon. minister is as perfect in his dealings with the public as he seems to think he is and that nothing of the kind I have referred to could occur. But I have heard it very frequently stated that these discriminations have been granted. I am not prepared to say whether that is correct or not. However, I think that if the railway commission is to be of use, it might as wejl apply to the government railways as to others. I see no reason why it should not apply to government railways. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) says that we are only now establishing a railway commission, that the system will be perfected by amendments from time to time, and that, some time, we may include express companies under the jurisdiction of this commission. But we are told that the United States have included express companies under their railway commission, and to this, the hon. member for Selkirk replies that the United States have had a railway commission in operation for years. Well, surely -we can learn by their experience. If they have brought express companies under the operation of the railway commission and are working out a successful system, it seems to me that we should take advantage of their experience rather than wait eight or ten years before we make this a part of our system. I do not see how we could hope for the best results in the operation of this law when, on the satne train you have certain cars with goods the rates of freight on which are regulated by the commission and also other cars with goods for which the carrier can charge exorbitant rates or make rates which discriminate in favour of the person as against another. I do not see any reason why all the goods carried on a train should not be under the protection, so far as rates are concerned, of this commission. The hon. minister speaks of it being so difficult to bring the express companies within the operation of the Bill. I listened carefully to his explanation, but I did not hear any explanation of what this difficulty was. The hon. minister says it would be troublesome, but in what respect it would be troublesome he did not inform us.

* I do not think there ever has been a Bill introduced in this House which was received with more general commendation than the one now under consideration. There is hardly a board of trade or an association interested in trade matters that has not approved of this Bill. The idea of a railway commission has been for twenty-five years, to a greater
or less extent, before parliament. Ever since I have had the honour of a seat in this House, there has been talk of introducing a railway commission Bill, but the idea has never come to maturity until now. The late government talked about a railway commission but they never actually introduced a Bill to establish it. The board of trade of Toronto sent a deputation to Ottawa which commended the Minister of Railways and Canals for the perfection of his Bill. It is true they suggested some amendment which they thought would improve the measure, but, if there was danger of the Bill not going through this session, they desired rather than that, to have no change made. It is probably right that a Bill of such importance as this should be criticised, but I rather think some of the criticism has gone a little too far. For my own part, I would like to see express companies brought under the operation of the Bill, and I have no doubt that, in time, this will be done. But as the Minister of Railways and Canals has pointed out, the Bill as it is covers them to a very large extent. And, if there is any danger that, in attempting to bring express companies under the operation of the Bill, the Bill itself would be made unworkable, we ought not to cumber the measure with such clauses. The hon. minister has intimated his wish that express companies should be placed under the control of this commission. But has pointed out that it would be better to do that by a separate Bill, which he purposes to introduce possibly this session, or, at all events next session. The hon. minister has given a great deal of care and attention to this Bill, and it is a Bill which ought to become law. It is supported, as I have said, by every public institution in the country. It is a Bill that has been petitioned for very widely and, as it stands it has been everywhere commended. Instead of our throwing obstructions in the way of the passage of the Bill we ought to help it along. Therefore, after the minister has given us the assurances we have heard, I think the member for East York (Mr. Maclean) should not pursue any further this hypercritical course in throwing out the little technical objections that he has been doing. One of the objections taken by the member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is that this Bill does not provide for provincial railways. How can he make it apply to provincial railways ? How can he make it apply to the railway being built by the Ontario government ? Every possible railway that it can be applied to will come under its jurisdiction. Therefore, instead of that being a reason against the Bill, I think it is a reason in its favour.
I did not give that as a reason why it should not be passed. I am not opposing the Bill, I am in favour of it; but I am endeavouring to point out its defects.

He pointed out that it would only apply, as he said, to a few railways at best-those were his words. Now, in point of fact there are only a few railways at best that It does not apply to. It does apply to 95 per cent of the railways in Canada; as to the other 5 per cent I understand the government have not power over them. I therefore think that the Bill should receive the support of the House. I believe it is a very good Bill, and the Minister of Railways deserves great compliments for bringing this measure before tiie House.

On more than one occasion I have endeavoured to find out, and I have not yet found out, on what grounds the Minister of Railways and Canals proposes to keep the government railways out of the jurisdiction of this commission. I can quite understand that the minister would prefer to run the government railways himself. He no doubt has more confidence in the present Minister of Railways and Canals than he would have in any commission, whether appointed by his own government or not. But we want to know why it is that the government railways should not be put under the jurisdiction of this commission just as the Grand Trunk Railway or any other railway will come under it. The hon. gentleman knows that if there is one thing that is particularly desirable in connection with this Bill, it is that wherever possible there shall be uniformity of regulation, uniformity of tariff, of rates and of every detail in the management of railways. It is of the utmost importance that there should be no line of demarcation between the several railways of the country, that the commission should not be restricted in their power to control the rates over all the railways in the country. When the public want to know what the rates are to be from Woodstock or Windsor to Halifax or St. John, the commission should be able to tell them and not be obliged to turn around and say: For a thousand miles of this railway we have nothing to say, that is under the control of the hon. gentleman who happens for the moment to be Minister of Railways and Canals, and of his officers. Now we have, of course, the highest respect for the present Minister of Railways and Canals. He has managed this railway so well for several years past that perhaps he considers he can do it a great deal better than any newly appointed commission. But the hon. gentleman may be a commissioner himself ; it has been so stated in the press, it is certainly a possibility ; and therefore we may have him as one of these gentlemen wlm are going to compose this commission, and we may have a new minister without any experience whatever. Surely the public would be better satisfied to have this commission, appointed for a series of years, and composed of experienced men with all the railway interests of the country under their charge, rather than have some portion Mr. SPROULE.
of the railway system under a minister for the time being who may not have had the slightest experience, and who may not possess our confidence in the same degree as the hon. minister who now occupies that position.
So far I have heard nothing from the minister on the subject except that he intends to omit government railways. Now surely, if the railways of this country are to be under a commission, and if it will be a benefit to the trading community that they shall be under this commission, we ought to know why it is that any portion of the railway mileage must be exempt. I would like to have that question answered. The hon. gentleman gave an answer a moment ago which he probably considered satisfactory. He said that in all the railway Acts that have been passed the government railways have been exempted. But what application has that to the present condition of things ? The hon. gentleman knows that in the past the general Railway Acts have not applied to government railways, in all their details, at all events, for the simple reason that all the other railways were worked by officers appointed by independent companies. Therefore there were restrictions upon the management and their officers that do not necessarily apply to government railways. But that is being all changed. We are no longer going to have the matters to be dealt with by this commission left in the hands of the various railway companies and their officers, they are going to be controlled by this commission, and why should not a railway operated by the government and its officers be controlled in like manner ? You are not proposing to interfere arbitrarily with the various railways, but you are proposing to interfere just so far as the public interest requires and to that extent the commission should have jurisdiction whether a railway is owned by a company or by government.
I may mention also that there are various things that will come under that commission as to which I am sure the public would feel safer in the hands of a commission than even in the hands of the hon. minister. I may recall to the minister that a short time ago there was a very serious accident upon the Intercolonial Railway, and there was an inquiry made into the accident. The minister, in referring to that in this House, spoke in the highest terms of commendation of the engine driver who was concerned in that accident, he gave a very high character to that man. Yet I understand that since then the investigation has shown that that man was not worthy of the commendation the minister gave him ; it was shown, as I understand, that he was a drinking man, and he had been drinking before he went upon the train, and was not in a fit condition to run the train. Now, all that took place under the management of the government. I ask why a railway that is sub-

ject to such accidents should be exempted from the commission which is to have jurisdiction as to all other railways. There are many other things that should come under the control of this commission besides the operation of the road and the control of tariffs and rates. The hon. gentleman does not provide for counsel appearing on behalf of either party when the commission are investigating matters upon the Intercolonial. The hon. gentleman is to be a law unto himself in that respect. He assumes that the trading community are going to be content with all the minister and his officers may do. But I can assure him that the trading community will not be content, they will be just as anxious to know every detail of the rates on the Intercolonial Railway as they will be to know the rates of any other railway in this country. I think we are entitled to know, not what the hon. gentleman wishes, but why it is that these government railways should not be under the control and jurisdiction of the commission.

Has it ever been suggested to him, may I ask the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, to put the matter of tolls, leaving out everything else in connection with the management of the Intercolonial Railway, under the jurisdiction of the commission ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAIRWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That has not received, the attention of the hon. minister ?
It has not been suggested.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I may draw the attention of the hon. minister again to this matter of classification to which I have referred. Although it has not been authorized by the Governor in Council and although it is not supposed to be a legal classification, yet, I notice that the Intercolonial Railway and Prince Edward Island Railway have consented to it with all the other railways, and that the name of one of the officers of the Intercolonial Railway is given as being one of the classification committee.
The MINISTER OB1 RAILWAYS AND CANALS. I can understand how that occurred. A joint committee composed of representatives from all the different railway companies meet periodically. I would not say that they meet at stated periods, but frequently meetings are held to consider traffic questions arising between them. I presume in this case they had a meeting in the usual way, and that they had agreed amongst themselves as to what they would recommend. It would devolve upon the companies that were moving to have the matter presented to the department for submission to and approval of by the Governor in Council. I do not blame the traffic officers for the issue of that, because that
would not properly be part of their duty. They only meet and agree upon what they think should be recommended. But, the department would not be committed in any way by any action of a traffic officer.

I quite understand the position, but in effect, under the Railway Commission, the government railways in respect of tolls will be subjected to the commission inasmuch as their officers who meet with the officers of other railways agree to this in joint committee, so that, the tolls on the Intercolonial Railway would be in effect under the jurisdiction of the commission, would they not ?
No, that Is only in reference to classification.
It has only reference to classification. The rates are another thing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The same officers agree to the rates as agree to the classification.
The rates which govern on the Intercolonial Railway are not the same rates which govern on other railways.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The government have a member on the classification committee and from time to time there is an alteration in the classification. The classification is sent up to the department for approval. No doubt this has been sent to the department month after month and has been neglected by the department and therefore has not got the necessary assent by Order in Council to confirm it. Perhaps that has occurred under other regimes as well as the present one, and after all if the classification is in accordance with the freight rates which have been approved of by the Governor in Council, if it does uot increase the rate upon any particular article, I do not think it requires the assent of the Governor in Council to it. If the classification has the effect of lessening the rate charged or leaving it at the same figure as before, I do not think it necessarily implies the assent of the Governor in Council to the new classification. The first think I did when I was minister was to inquire from the officers of the department if the new classification had the effect of increasing the rates or tolls which had been charged before, and if it did not have that effect, I do not think the officers went to the trouble of having an Order in Council passed to confirm the classification.
