I think thel statute says that all rates and tolls have to be approved by the Governor in Council and that any new classification must be in accordance with the last classification approved of by the Governor in Council.

The last classification was the eleventh that was promulgated by the railway company, and approved by the Governor

in Council. I think it is necessary under the Act that each classification as it comes out, if it varies from the previous one, as of course it must, otherwise they would not issue a new one, must be approved. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Ilaggart) suggests that probably the companies might have sent this classification into the department and that it has been overlooked. 1 am informed that it has not been submitted to the department at all, and even if it had been submitted and overlooked that would not warrant them in issuing a new classification and taking action upon it. The law reads :
The company in fixing or regulating the tolls to be demanded and taken for the transportation of goods, shall, exicept in respect to through traffic to or from the United States, adopt and conform to any uniform classification of freight which the Governor in Council on the report of the minister from, time to time, prescribes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What clause is that ?

No. 220. Some hon. gentlemen are complaining because they say I have not given them any sufficient explanation of why I pointed out that the inclusion of express companies by express terms could not be made in this Bill. I will try to repeat myself and make it clear if hon. gentlemen really desire information on the subject. I have said that the present Bill, I think, covers the subject quite fully now. It does not deal with all express companies. It only, by imputation, deals with the express companies which do their business upon railways. So far as the receipts of express companies are made up of railway charges and charges in respect to carriage upon railways, these charges are entirely within the control of the railway commission under this Bill. I am not prepared to say that the commission could not compel the carriage of these goods by the express company or by the railway company through the agency of the express companies who are using the trains to carry these goods at such a price as the railway commission might determine. The present Bill goes as far as we can properly go with respect to railways. The express company end of the thing is another matter. Possibly an express company might be justified in making some additional charge for removing goods from a warehouse or dwelling to a railway, or from the railway to their destination. Perhaps an express company might properly make some charge in respect to the oversight of goods in transit, but so far as the railway carriage is concerned, that is subject absolutely to the control of the railway commission under this Bill. I have seen the language of some of these clauses in the United States legislation, and I can understand how they deal with express companies. One cogent reason would be, that some of these Bills are Bills for the purpose of Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
regulating tolls and charges which are imposed by common carriers. The definition of * common carriers ' Is determined by a long series of judicial decisions, and under our law common carriers have not the same liabilities and are not the same people as common carriers in the United States. The relative rights and duties of common carriers are largely dependent upon the common law in this country and in the United States, and in the United Kingdom, modified to some extent by statute. We could not say that express companies in their express business shall be subject to the control of this Bill without setting up a machinery to provide for it. Express companies send by steamers as well as by railways and perhaps by horses and wagons, and if you are going to control their business it would be necessary to provide machinery for so doing. There is no common sense in putting in a clause saying that express companies shall be controlled in their rates by this railway commission when you have not any machinery prescribed, at all events for dealing with that portion of their business which is not carried by the railroad. If we limit or restrict the business of express companies which do tlieir business by railroad, don't you think they would have reason to complain that we loft a free hand to express companies who transacted business through other agencies.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If freight is carried partly by railroad and partly by water, don't you give the commission the power to apportion the rates to each.

Yes, but that does not touch the fringe of the question. As an illustration, the steamers between Montreal and Quebec do an express business, and so do the railways between these two points. You would have control over the one and not over the other, and if the express companies who did their business by railroad were to complain that they were restricted by legislation and that the water carriers were free, there would appear to be some reasonableness in that complaint. It appears to me that you can only properly deal with the control of express companies by independent legislation. If you insert it in this Bill, you will have to string all the way through the Bill provisions which will exempt certain clauses from application to them, and that would simply complicate the Bill and make it difficult of operation. I give my honest conviction to gentlemen opposite, whether they accept it or not. that this is a matter that can only be satisfactorily and properly dealt with by separate legislation. This Bill has reference to railways and all questions connected witii railways that effect the public interest. It is not simply to control rates on railways, but its provisions govern the incorporation of companies, the construction of railways, the protection which is afforded to the pub-

lie by railways, the operation of railways in all their various departments ; and it would be a mistake to thrust a clause into it to say that the Bill shall apply to express companies without looking ahead to see what other alterations will have to be made and what additional machinery may be required. I have no objection at all on principle to the control of express companies. I think it would fee a proper thing to have power to control express companies, but let us do it in the right way. If we do it, let us do it efficiently.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Would the minister allow me to make this suggestion which would meet his objection :
This Act shall apply to all persons, companies and railways Including the express business of such railways.
That would not do.

Of course I have had no opportunity of considering the bearing of that amendment, but this thought occurs to me ; Why should you throw the express business out of the railways and into other hands, which would be the result of that amendment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I think that this matter of express companies could be dealt with in four lines without * affecting the general scope of the Bill. The hon. minister seems to think it would be necessary to extensively change its wording. I am advised by a very eminent lawyer that the addition of the following few words would accomplish what we want in regard to express companies :
Section 2, subsection C. The expression 'company' means a railway company and express company and includes any person having authority to construct or. operate a railway or express company.
Section 3, subsection 4. Sections 1 to 50 inclusive, and 251 to 280 inclusive, only shall apply to express companies.

I do not know whether the eminent lawyer my hon. friend refers to has been asked to express an opinion whether or not the present Bill does not practically control all rates that are levied for railroad carriage of every kind and description. Has that question been asked by the hon. gentleman ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I may state that it was Mr. Staunton, who waited on the hon. minister with some other gentlemen, who framed that proposed amendment. He informed me that it would cover the whole case. The hon. minister must believe that Mr. Staunton is very sincere in his desire to see this Bill become law, and he would not make that statement unless he was sure of his ground.

I am sure that Mr. Staunton
would not express that opinion unless he was assured in his own mind that he was right, and I am sure also that he is in sympathy with the Bill and desires it to become law. All the same, I am not prepared at this moment to express the opinion that express companies would not be as adequately covered by the Bill without that provision as with it, unless there were other provisions. There is no doubt whatever that other provisions would have to be incorporated to make this Bill, as a Bill, operative upon express companies, stronger than it is now- ; and, moreover, after you had done that, you would only have reached a portion of the express business and a portion of the express companies. It is a matter which I think this parliament ought seriously to consider, whether, when we are dealing with express companies, we ought not to deal with them as a whole. I cannot see what justification we can possibly have for dealing with them by instalments, or for dealing with a portion of their business, and not with the balance of it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman propose to deal with them as common carriers ?
We cannot, because we are not legislating on the subject of common carriers here.	-
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I mean in any proposed Bill to deal with them as a whole.

If the minister says this is a question worth consideration, I am willing to leave it for the present, especially if it is to be taken up in connection with the amendments suggested by Mr. Staunton, to provide for jurisdiction over the charges of express companies, which are, as a matter of fact, a subject of common complaint throughout the country.

I am willing to let this section stand, if hon. gentlemen want to think more about it. But I would like those who wish to come to a direct conclusion on the subject to seek an opinion from those who may be expected to know, whether or not this Bill, as it is now framed, does not comprehensively cover the case of express companies, as respects the carriage of express merchandise on railways.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Oh, yes, it does that.

Then you cannot make the Bill go any further by providing in specific terms that it shall apply to express companies, because you would have to include other provisions in order that the commission could deal with express companies in their business on other routes and conveyances than railways.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister's Bill may provide for the carriage of articles by express on railways, but that does not reach the question at all. Suppose an article is put in an express company's office twelve miles from a railway. It has to be carried to the railway station, and there should be an allowance for that and for warehousing as well as for the carriage on the railway. That principle is admitted in the Bill, because it gives to the commission power to apportion railway freights as distinct from lake and ocean freights. Otherwise the thing would be useless in the case of an article shipped partly by lake or ocean and partly by rail. In the same way you would have to give to the commissioners power to apportion so much for the carriage to the station and for the warehousing as well as for carriage by rail.
You would need to have provisions inserted for determining that, and you would then be dealing only with a certain portion of the business of express companies.
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do I understand the minister to argue that under the Bill as it is now the commission would have authority and power to regulate the express rates so far as the goods were carried on a railway ?
Yes, certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If that is the case, it covers 99 per cent of the goods shipped by express, because only a very small fraction of the goods so shipped are not shipped entirely on railways ; and the argument that express companies ought to be exempt from the operations of the Act because you could not cover their entire operations, is in exact contradiction to the argument that this Act is a good Act with regard to railways although it does not cover government railways, and some other lines of railway. If the Bill is a good one with respect to the operations of railways, although it does not cover them all, it seems to me it would he an excellent Act if it covered the operations of express companies on railways alone, because 99 per cent of the goods are carried on railways, not on water or by wagon.

The suggestion of the hon. Minister of Railways is a fair one. He proposes to let clause 3 stand in order to see whether the proposition I have made can be adopted. It wasi not clear to Mr. Staunton that the wording of the Act covered express freights on railways.
What part of the Act is it which the hon. minister thinks covers the express business ? I do not find anything in the interpretation clause to lead to that conclusion. The word ' com-

pany ' is interpreted to ai railway company and to include any person having authority to construct or operate a railway. By no stretch of the imagination can we say that that includes express companies. Nor can it come under the interpretation of the word ' railway.' It would be well if the hon. minister would point out what particular part of the Act he relies on for his opinion that express companies are included.

I do not think that I need particularize any one or more sections of the Bill. Take the sections between 251 and 280. This Bill gives to a railway commission power to say what shall be the tolls exacted by railways on every article of traffic. That is pretty comprehensive to start with. The commission need not wait for the railway company to say how* much it wants to charge but may arbitrarily fix what the toll shall be. We do not discriminate between goods carried by an express company and those which are not. Every article carried on a railway must get, in respect of the tolls levied, the approval of thq commission.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister has given in his Bill a special definition to the word ' railway ' and the definition will exclude express companies.

Not at all. An argument of that kind would result in this. All that a railway company would have to do in order to shirk its responsibility and escape the control of the commission would be, instead of carrying its goods itself, to carry them in the name of an outside corporation-call it an express company or agency company or anything you like.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is why we want express companies included.

What is the particular advantage of indicating any one company by name any more than any other ? When you say that this Act shall apply to all persons, companies and railways, other than government railways, what more do you want ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman ought to readjust his interpretation clause. He is giving a limited definition to those words ' persons, companies and railways.'
You will findi no limitation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The word ' railway,' in the interpretation clause, means any railway which the company has authority to construct or operate, and that word ' company ' means a company operating a railway.

In the third clause, this Act ap-

plies to all persons, companies and railways other than government railways. Of course that means all companies operating railways, and when it means that, it means as well all companies doing business on railways and getting benefit out of the carriage of goods on railways.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It would not mean a company carrying on a book-selling business on a railway ?
No, there are no freight rates in that business.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: By your definition of the word ' companies,' it includes any person having authority to construct or operate a railway. Express companies do not operate railways.

That does not affect the case. The Bill applies to all persons, companies and railways. If you can suggest anybody who is not comprised in one or the other of these, there might be some reason for changing the Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will it cover telephone companies ?
They have not anything necessarily to do with railways.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This Act applies to all persons.
Yes, that have to do with railways,, that are operating, owning or carrying goods on railways.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It does not say anything about carrying companies. It says ' any person having authority to construct or to operate a railway.'
That is the definition of the word ' company.' The Bill, in its provisions, does apply to all persons, companies and railways.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Section 278 rather implies that express companies have a different meaning. It says :	' Every company '-
that would mean a railway company-'which grants any facilities for the carriage of goods by express to any incorporated express company or person, shall grant equal facilities on equal terms and conditions, to any other incorporated express company which demands the same.' That rather implies that the general scope of the Act does not cover express companies.

Not necessarily. This provision is included in order that there may be no advantage given to any express company over another. If you will take the clauses with regard to traffic and tolls and all that, you will gather this clearly from them, that
no traffic can be carried on railways nor can any tolls or charges be imposed in respect of the carriage of such traffic, until the Railway Commission has said what these tolls shall be. Now, if the railway company itself cannot do that, it cannot by any contract that it may make or any authority it may delegate to anybody else, authorize some other person to do it. Any person or company who may, by the authority and permission of the railway company, have any special privileges in respect of the carriage of traffic over that railway can only exercise that special privilege subject to the control of the railway company. Otherwise all that would be necessary would be for the railway to hand its freight business over to another company and it would thereby avoid all control. That, I think, should be thoroughly understood, and it is so clear that it ought to be accepted. If the law does not mean that it is not worth the paper it is printed on even to control business carried on railways outside of that managed by the express companies.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the hon. minister means what he says, why not amend clause c, of the interpretation clause, so as to cover distinctly what he says ?
I do not think that any amendment is needed at all. If hon. gentlemen will look further on in the Act, they will see the word ' companies '-
The amendment would be needed if you want to control the express business outside of railways.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Quite so. Clause c, of the Interpretation Act says that the expression ' company ' means a railway company. If hon. gentlemen will look through the Act they will find the word ' company ' here and there throughout the whole length of it. But clause 3 says :
This Act shall apply to all persons, companies and railways.
-and so on. That word ' companies ' there has no reference to the Interpretation clause of the Act
Surely.

Certainly it has not, and I think I can give my hon. friend very ample authority for my position. This is the word ' companies ' which is not interpreted by the interpretation clause, but the word that is interpreted is ' company ' and that occurs throughout the length and breadth of the Act, and is interpreted to mean a railway company.
And it has a capital ' C.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Certainly. The word ' company ' in the third clause has not the restricted meaning given in the interpretation clause, but has the same meaning as

it would have in any other Act passed by this parliament. So when we say ' all persons, companies and railways ' we mean exactly what we say, that all these are subject to the Act.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. German) mean that the interpretation clause applies only to the singular of the word ' company ' and not to the plural ? That Is what his argument means.

Certainly, that is exactly what I mean. Here you have the interpretation of a word, the word ' company ' and that word is carried throughout the whole Act, and is interpreted to mean a railway company. X venture to say the word ' companies ' is also used here and there throughout the Act, and that where it does not come within the meaning of the Railway Act it is a general term whicli covers all companies and is not intended to be restricted by the interpretation clause.

Does not the hon. member for Lincoln and Niagara (Mr. Lancaster) know -1 am sure he does, but he has not profited by the knowledge-that in the general Interpretation Act governing ail statutes the very word ' person ' means company as well as individual ?
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I know that very well. But the hon. minister is not content with the general Interpretation Act, but proposes special interpretation clauses for his own Act, which he is asking us to approve. If he is not satisfied with the general Interpretation Act, we suppose that lie regards these interpretations that he proposes as having special significance. In reply to what the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) says, I know very well the difference in the interpretation whicli he speaks of, but this Act expressly states what a railway shall mean and what the word ' company ' shall mean. But I do not agree with him when he says that the word 1 company ' has a different significance in the singular from what it has in the plural.
Has the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) read the Bill ?
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I have read it all through three or four times.
The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND Canals. Is the hon. gentleman of opinion that, if this Bill becomes law, any railway company in Canada can carry goods or allow goods to be carried on its line without first having arranged for tolls and tariffs approved or authorized by the railway commission 1

Not quite in the way the hon. minister puts it. But I want to point out that, in my humble opinion, the way to provide for what he desires is not by giving a special interpretation to the Mr. GERMAN.
word ' company.' If he wants to make his Bill apply to the carrying of all traffic on railways, the natural, simple and efficacious way is to say that it shall apply to express companies that are carrying goods on railways.

Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) seriously tell this House that a railway company, if this Bill were in force, could not carry goods at rates fixed without the authority of the commission, but that it could authorize an agent to do so ?
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No ; but one way of reaching the point may be much more cumbersome than another. And if you wish to make the Act apply easily, quickly and cheaply, as it is in the interest of the country that it should do, to traffic carried on railways, the Act should be simple and direct, and should leave no question that the express companies, if they do carry freight, carry it as the agents of the railway company. We all seem to agree as to what should happen, but we disagree as to the way of getting at it. I submit to the hon. minister that he should put it beyond doubt by saying that express companies shall be in the same position as the railways.

I do not think it would be creditable legislation to us to attempt to remove doubts that do not exist. If the hon. gentleman admits that a railway company cannot carry goods over its line without being subject to the provisions of this law, he has not a leg to stand on, so far as the charges on express business carried on railways are concerned. And that is all we propose to deal with under this Bill. The hon. gentleman says it would be better and simpler to deal with the express companies as agents of the railway companies. I contend that it is simpler and better to deal witlf one company, the railway company, than to deal with a company and also with its agent. The railway company is responsible, under severe penalties under this clause, for any departure from the rates fixed by the commission. You do not want to deal with anybody else but the railway company. So far as it is necessary and proper to control the express companies in connection with the railways, they are controlled by this Bill. When you speak of general control of express companies you have not got it here, and you cannot put it here without embarrassing the Bill and im-paring its value by introducing what is really an outside element, something that had better be dealt with in a separate and distinct measure.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I would just like to put a case to the hon. minister. Suppose that goods to be carried in charge of an express company start on a railway in my county. The railway I refer to is not one

of the railways included under this Act, it is not within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada. It is an electric railway which carries fruit, and runs from the county of Lincoln
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to correct him ? When he speaks of the Niagara Central, that is under the control of the Dominion parliament.

I am not talking about the Niagara Central, I am talking about an Ontario electric railway. I said a railway not included in this Act. I refer to the Hamilton, Grimsby and Beamsville Electric Railway, and that road never had any connection whatever with the Niagara Central, which is now the Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto railway, running from Port Dalhousie to Niagara Falls. But the Hamilton, Grimsby and Beamsville Electric Railway starts at the village of Beamsville and runs through a fruit growing belt to the city of Hamilton. That is an electric railway only incorporated under an Ontario Act, and is in no sense covered by this clause three. Now, the question I want to put to the minister is this :	Suppose some
constituent of mine ships his fruit on that electric railway to be carried to Ottawa. It is to be carried by the Dominion Express Company that starts on the Hamilton. Grimsby and Beamsville Electric Railway and is then transferred to the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is a railway within the provisions of this Act ? Now, what does the minister say about that express business ? Wher(e the traffic in the goods originates on a railway not under the operation of this Act if this transfer occurs on their journey, whether the commissioners that look after this traffic are to do anything to help the shipper, because they must look after the goods on their whole journey from beginning to end. Now, would not the minister do better to say that this express business should be dealt with under this Act, that this Act should apply to any express company that carries goods on either an electric or a steam railway and whether such railway is or is not one of the railways covered by this Act ? Because in the case of fruit growers I have mentioned they do not ship their goods on a railway which is within the authority of this Act, their goods go twenty or twenty-five miles before they reach a railway that is within the authority of this Act. I think that class of cases ought to be provided for, and would be covered by the amendment such as I have suggested.

I do not wish to do the hon. gentleman any discourtesy, but I would recommend him to read the Bill, because when he reads the Bill he will find that the case he refers to is entirely covered by section five. There the hon. gentleman will
find that the moment a through shipment is made and it is transferred to the Canadian Pacific Railway, then the rate must be a through rate and will be controlled by the commission. But I am ready to consider the suggestion that has been made. In any case, I would now move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

On section 11,

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Section 11 has been amended to read as follows :
11. The directors may issue as paid-up stock, shares of the capital stock of the company in payment for all or any of the businesses, franchises, undertakings, rights, powers, privileges, and properties which the company may lawfully acquire by this Act or by law, and may, for such considerations, allot and hand over such shares to any person or corporation, including its shareholders or its directors, and any such issue or allotment of stock shall be binding upon the company and such stock shall not be assessable for calls nor shall the holder thereof be liable in any way thereon ; or the company may pay for the same wholly or partly in paid-up shares or wholly or partly in debentures, as may be agreed upon ; provided that any allotment and issue of stock under authority of this section shall be approved by the holders of at least two-thirds in value of the stock of the company, previously issued and held at the date of such issue and allotment.

I would like to ask any hon. gentleman who was in the committee whether or not he has examined similar provisions made in previous Bills in reference to the handing out of stock of this kind in payment. It does not seem to me that the clause safeguards the enterprise at all because the shareholders might hand over the stock for a mere nominal consideration. They might pass it over for a song and if the stockholders are all interested in one way, that is, in getting a distribution of stock among themselves, there is nothing to prevent it being done under that clause as it stands. I do not think it has been well considered.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is the usual clause.

I am quite sure it is not the

usual clause because there is no provision to safeguard the transaction, except the consent of two-thirds of the other stockholders shall be had. Is it desirable or not that we should confer the power upon any company that we incorporate here to hand over its stock for nothing if it chooses ? If two: thirds of the stockholders are prepared to give the stock out without any valuable consideration being received in return upon any terms which they choose, it is a question whether this is a desirable clause to incorporate in the Bill or not. That is my proposition and if it has been well considered perhaps there will be some bon. member of the committee who has had the matter in charge or was present when the discussion took place who could throw some light upon it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That clause was not originally in this Bill, but when it came before the Private Bills Committee the acting chairman at that time, one of the hon. members for Ottawa, proposed that the original clause should be struck out and that this clause be inserted, being exactly in line with a clause in a Bill which the Private Bills Committee had passed the day before. I do not see very much difference between this clause and the one that had been originally in, but I was quite willing to accept it and the committee passed it. The hon. member for Montreal, St. Lawrence, (Mr. Bickerdike) bad a Bill with this same clause in it which had passed the Private Bills Committee. When it was considered by the Private Bills Committee it was thought that this clause should be adopted.

I do not think there is much difference between the two clauses. I think there should be something in this clause which will require the transaction to be a bona fide transaction, not a mere nominal transaction, but a bona fide one in which bona fide value is being given for the stock. That is not secured by this present Bill. I do not think the new clause is any better than its predecessor. They are both open to the same exception.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: So far as the promoters of the Bill are concerned they are not objecting at all to any reasonable amendment that the hon. minister, or any one else, desires to put in to ensure that it shall be a bona fide transaction. The gentlemen who are asking for incorporation are going into it in a bona fide way and they are willing to have any restrictions placed around them that are reasonable and that other companies are bound to submit to.
There is no such clause in the General Company's Act and no such clause would be admitted in the General Company's Act, I am quite sure.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What would you suggest ?

I am not prepared at the moment to frame a clause. There will no doubt arise circumstances under which stock might be handed over for property which was being acquired in a bona fide way for the interests of the company. If any person wanted to put through a transaction which was not a bona fide transaction, but simply a cover to the getting possession of the stock, with a properly framed clause, the stock might be taken away from them and proceedings might be taken which would invalidate the transaction, but they could not be under this clause as it stands.
Mi-. SPROULE. It seems to me that it is doubly dangerous for this reason :	In
clause four the capital stock which the company may issue is placed a't 85,000,000. They can divide that as they see fit so long as shareholders representing two-thirds of the capital stock agree. Then they can issue bonds to the extent of $5,000,000 and deal with them afterwards. With the provisions in clauses 4, 11 and 13 it seems to me to be susceptible of a good deal of stock jobbery if they were disposed to go into it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This Bill was drawn in an exactly similar way to the Bill incorporating the Hamilton and Lake Erie Power Company, which was obtained from this parliament in 1895. The clause originally drafted was taken verbatim from the act to incorporate the Hamilton and Lake Erie Power Company. I had supposed in drafting the Bill that what had been done on a former occasion by this parliament would be done again.
You might reasonably do so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: One might reasonably suppose that. The company does not desire anything more than what is fair, and they intend to go into the project in a bona fide way if they go into it at all. Engineers have already looked over the ground and it is supposed to be a feasible and profitable proposition, and having taken this clause' verbatim from a Bill which has already passed parliament, I cannot see why there should be objection to it.
Perhaps we should have a model clause.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think there should be a clause common to all Bills, but if some such words as ' bona fide ' are inserted here, I do not see what objection there can be to the wording of the clause as it stands at present. If any party is willing to take stock in payment, then when two-thirds of the shareholders say that it is a good bargain rather than to give cash, I do not see what harm there is in it.
Suppose they should be all in a ring.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then they would have to be In league with the parties who are giving them the franchise. It often happens that a corporation can make a better bargain with parties who are willing to take stock than if they have to go on the market and get cash. If you wish, let there be some safeguarding words in this section which will apply to similar Bills through all time.

If you strike out the words in the clause ' may make and ' and leave it that the directors ' may issue as paid up and non assessable shares ' I think it would meet all objections. The moment the stock is paid up, is it material to any one what they do with it ?

I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. Bickerdike) apprehends the full extent of my objection. Even if these words be struck out it would still be possible for the company to issue as paid up and assessable stock any amount they please without getting anything in return.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I want to guard against that.

As a member of the Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills I am glad that this, question has come up. Bills of this kind invariably contain a similar clause and on every occasion there is considerable discussion in the committee. The clause now before the House is the clause as amended by the committee, and we adopted it on the ground that it has been inserted in many Bills already and is looked upon as a model clause. If the House in committee should now rule as to what is a proper clause for such Bills it would save a great deal of the time of the committee and act as a guide. I cannot say that I have much objection to the clause as it stands. As the member for Guysborough has said, it is sometimes advantageous for the company to purchase real estate or other things by means of stock, and if there is any way in which the clause may be limited so as to overcome the possibility of fraud might be well to insert that limitation.
If the hon. gentleman prefers, I am willing to have a clause drafted and submit it for consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Surely there can be no objection to the company issuing stock as paid up stock for the construction of buildings, the purchasing of franchises or of any property as contemplated by this section. I infer from what the minister says that this is legitimate so long as the transaction is a bona fide one, and that if they are getting value they can pay for it in stock
or in money. If people enter Into a project with the intention of committing fraud it is very hard to prevent them from doing so by legislation, and if any clause can he devised whereby you can prevent persons from being guilty of fraud who desire to commit fraud, I -would like to see it, because I have never seen it yet. What is there wrong about issuing paid up shares in a company as consideration for a contract for the construction say of a race-way that would cost $1,000,000? Why should not the contractors be allowed to take stock in the company just as well as forcing the company to raise the money to pay the contractors ? So long as you accede to the principle that the company may in a bona fide way issue stock as a consideration for payment of a contract or any franchises or privileges, I do not see how you can prevent them doing wrong if they want to do it. I doubt very much if it could be done. I am quite willing that the Bill should stand over, and if the minister can devise a clause that will meet the case, I should be satisfied.

I do not wish it to be inferred that I took the position that a power of this kind might not be very properly and honestly exercised ; but what I did say was that this clause as it stands is peculiarly liable to abuse. The only condition attached to it is that two-thirds of the stockholders shall be consenting parties to the transaction. That is no protection at all. What I thought, and still think, would be an ingredient that would greatly militate against the use of this section in a fraudulent way, would be to include in it such terms as would practically make the transaction void if it were not in compliance with the ternis of the section. If the parties to the transaction knew that it was liable to be attacked in the courts and set aside on that ground, I think they would hesitate.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would not the non-compliance of the transaction with the provisions of the clause not render it void ipso facto ? Does the minister mean that if all the formalities of the clause were not complied with, the transaction would be void ?

I have not thought about the proper wording of the clause ; but there is nothing in it as it stands that could not be complied with, and yet the thing might be the most fraudulent transaction in the world.
Progress reported.

speechtext:

The MINISTER OF MIIdTIA AND DEFENCE. ~I scarcely expected to be asked to make that exxilanation to-night. It is to be regretted that we should not have had the Bill, notice of which was given on the 3rd of April, before taking up these estimates. I recognize that the hon. Minister of Militia is entitled to some indulgence, but this year we have reason to expect considerable changes in the militia organization. The committee will remember that during the colonial conference in London, engagements were entered into by our representatives at that conference, and we are entitled to know how far the government intend adhering to those engagements, and what changes are contemplated. Under the circumstances, it is to be regretted that we have not had from the Minister of Militia some outline of all the changes he contemplates. We have estimates to the extent of over a million and a half dollars, and it would be more satisfactory if we knew in a general way, before voting those estimates, what new schemes the government may have in view. Another matter to which I wish to refer is this:	I
would like to know if the militia who were called out during the strike in Yalleyfield, a considerable time ago, have been paid by the government or not ? On the 11th of this month some questions were put regarding this matter, which will be found on page 2759 of ' Hansard.' Among those questions, which were put by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin), were these :
Were the militia ordered out at Valleyfleld at the time of the strike ? If so, what was the cost of the troops ? By whom was the said cost paid ? Has the town of Valleyfleld paid the costs ?
In the absence of the hon. Minister of Militia, the Postmaster General replied :
The mayor of Valleyfleld made a requisition for the services of the militia on October 25th af the request of the company, and two companies of infantry arrived in Valleyfleld from Montreal that night.
And in reply to the other questions, the Postmaster General said :
The Department of Labour has no information on the subjects referred to In these questions.
The questions were not put to the Department of Labour nor to the Minister of Labour, nor to the Postmaster General, hut were put generally to the government, and I think that the answer given was neither fair nor sincere, because, from the Information I have gathered, the troops on that occasion-just before the elections of 1900-



were paid by the government, and no claim lias since been enforced against the town of Valley field for reimbursement. If such be the case, I submit that the answer given was neither sincere nor true. There is another matter to which I wish to refer. Recently at Montreal the troops were [DOT]called out, not to protect any private industry as in the case of the Valleyfield riot, but to protect the shipping interests of the country. I am informed that the militia have not yet been paid. Some of the officers are even out of pocket. It is only just that these troops should be paid at once, and that the cost should fail, not on the city of Montreal, but on this government, if there is any strength in the Valleyfield precedent. In Valleyfield the troubles were between the men employed in the mill of the company and the company itself, whereas, in Montreal the troubles were of a far more public character. Troops were called out to protect the harbour, which is to a large extent under the jurisdiction of this government, and I think that, under the circumstances, the cost should not be saddled on the city of Montreal, but should be paid by the government. These are questions to which we are entitled to an answer. We are entitled to know whether the reply given by the hon. Postmaster General on the 11th of May is correct or not, whether the government have definitely assumed the cost of calling out the troops at Valleyfield, and what is the intention of the government with regard to the cost incurred at Montreal ?

I do not think the hon. gentleman has any right to charge insincerity in the answer given. It so happened that I was not in the city the day that question was put, and until this moment, my attention has not been called to the nature of the answer given. I gave instructions that the question should be answered and the answer sent to the Prime Minister, but possibly through some inadvertence that was not done. There is not the slightest objec-tition to answering the question. The government paid the men, of course. If the hon. gentleman will take the trouble to look at the law governing the case, he will see that it provides that when two magistrates or the mayor of the city make a requisition on the senior officer to call out the troops, in case of riot, the expense is paid by the city or the municipality interested, but where, for any reason, the pay is not immediately forthcoming, the Act authorizes the government to pay the men, and the officer in command, upon whom the requisition was made, then proceeds to sue the municipality for the amount. That is the law. In the case of the town of Valleyfield, the men were paid out of the consolidated revenue fund, and I understand that the commanding officer is taking the necessary steps for the return of the money. I do not know. That is beyond Mr. MONK.
my control ; I have nothing to do with it. So far as the city of Montreal is concerned, the law, of course, is precisely the same as I have just quoted. There is not a question whether it is shipping or a government building or anything else that is to be protected ; it is simply a question of the violation of the peace. That having taken place and a riot threatening, the Act enables the chief magistrate of a municipality to call upon the militia to protect the citizens. That was done in the city of Montreal. If the men have not been paid they will be paid under the authority contained in the Act which I have quoted. I was informed on Saturday morning by my deputy that the accounts had not yet been forwarded to him, but that he had made inquiry into the matter, and, so soon as the accounts were forwarded to him they would be paid under the authority I have mentioned, if, in the meantime, the city had not chosen to pay them; and then, of course, the same proceeding I have mentioned in the former case, th& usual proceedings, would be taken-the officer in command of the troops would sue to recover the amount of money paid.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Do I understand the hon. minister (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) to say that no claim has been received from the military authorities in Montreal for the pay of the militia ?
I said that up to Saturday last no accounts, no claim of any kind, had been received here at headquarters.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

tion ; he is obliged to bring action under the law.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: But these officers are under the control of the department; and it should not surprise the committee if, under the circumstances of this case of the town of Val-leyfield, I should claim that it is the duty of the government to see to it that these soldiers who served in Montreal are paid without delay, and also that a different rule should not be applied to the city of Montreal from that which has been applied to the town of Valleyfield. The mere fact that there happened to be a by-election in one place and not in the other should not make a difference in the application of the law. I do not ask that Valleyfield should be obliged to contribute to the pay of the militia, but I do find it unjust that the city of Montreal, which contributes more to the revenue of this country than does the town of Valleyfield, should be subjected to a different rule from that which was applied in this other case.

I wish to enter a protest at this stage about this matter. If the militia were called out in Valleyfield to suppress a riot and the government paid the cost 'of the maintenance of those soldiers while on duty, the same rule should apply to the city of Toronto. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk)'is quite right in demanding that no exceptional treatment should be given any municipality. Some time last summer, I think it was, the militia were called to do duty in the city of Toronto owing to an anticipated riot because of a street car strike, and the city of Toronto was called upon to pay the necessary expenses in connection with the presence of those troops there. Now, this unfortunate trouble in Valleyfield took place about three years ago. I presume that the men were paid immediately after their service. Surely some officer of the department instructed the commanding officer to proceed to collect this money. Or, are we simply bandying words about this business ? It is time that we should know whether one rule is to be applied to Valleyfield because a byelection was coming on, while another rule must apply to other municipalities. If the law is that the municipality is to pay for the troops, that law should be enforced.

My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) will see that there is no way by which the commanding officer can force a municipality to immediately hand over the money if the municipality does not see fit to do so. In the case of Toronto, evidently the city authorities felt that they were hound to pay and they did pay. That has happened in a great many other cases, in the city of London, for instance. The town of Valleyfield -and the same has happened in other cases -there was hesitation and delay about paying. Of course, the men had to be paid, and,

under the authority given in the Act, the government advanced the money.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: But three years have elapsed since the money was paid, and surely some steps should be taken, if it is the duty of the municipality to pay.

Here is what the law says. In the event of the money being advanced by the government out of the consolidated revenue fund, then the commanding officer shall at once, in his own name, proceed against the municipality for the recovery of such sum.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Then is the officer commanding the troops who were called out still in command ?

I am not quite sure whether Colonel Gorden, who is the officer commanding at Montreal now, was in Montreal at that time. I think he was in South Africa, and that Colonel Roy was commanding at that time. But I will get a statement upon this point, and bring down the exact condition of affairs, when the estimates next come up.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Will instructions be issued that this money shall be collected ?
My impression is that steps have already been taken to collect it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I am not satisfied with the answer of the minister. I do not find fault because the government paid the money, it is a proper thing for the government to pay in the meantime if the municipality does not. But now nearly three years have gone by, and we are voting the estimates to-day, and the minister does not know. I do not accept his statement that it was none of his business. It is not only his business, but it is his duty as head of the Militia Department who are out this money, to take steps to collect it. I go further, and I say that we have no right to remit the money, and if any such steps were taken at the time as have been spoken of, they were taken beyond the authority of the law. The government could not pay this by Order in Council. Therefore, I do not accept the minister's statement that it is not his duty to know. Is it to be understood that when a municipality refuses to pay, the government is to assume the debt ? Supposing Toronto had declined to pay, suppose Montreal should decline to pay now, the government should promptly see that the proper steps are taken to collect the money. It is not the duty of the commanding officer, because he is immediately under the control of the Department of Militia and Defence, he is only acting as the trustee of the government, or of the department. Therefore, when these estimates come up we have a constitutional right to

insist upon this explanation. I was surprised at the trivial answer of the Postmaster General, or the Minister of Labour. Everybody knew that he had no business to answer, it was not his place to do so. It was his place to say, the Minister of Militia and Defence is not here to-day, let the matter stand, and it would have stood as a matter of course. Then if the Postmaster General, or the Minister of Labour, had not interfered to give that answer, the Minister of Militia and Defence would have given us the information and we would not have been compelled to ask the government for it on another occasion. I say the language of my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) is none too strong in characterizing that answer as unsatisfactory and trivial. Look at the result. If he had communicated with the Minister of Militia and Defence and informed him of what had happened, the Minister of Militia and Defence would have inquired and this discussion to-night would have been avoided. Now, I must say that since I have been in opposition I have not engaged in any obstruction; but I want my hon. friend to understand that I propose to be severe in my criticisms when necessity calls for it, and when the government endeavour to trifle with us I wont stand it. So far as I am concerned, if the minister will give us this information it will be satisfactory, but I do not accept his explanation that it was not his fault that the answer was given in that way.
I certainly will do as I promised, and bring down a statement with regard to this matter.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Will he bring down a statement as to whether his department or the Justice Department, or the Labour Department, has instructed the proper officials to proceed against the municipality to collect this money ?
There was no need of any instructions under the law.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Will the minister bring down a memorandum explaining exactly how the matter stands, so that we may know what steps this House may take, if necessary, to have that money collected ?

The money of the country is controlled by the Minister of Finance, and the moment the Minister of Finance consents to an extraordinary expenditure of this kind, he debits somebody with that amount of money and he never rests until he gets that money back. He calls on the Department of Militia and Defence at least once a week to know whether they have recovered that money. If the business of the department is conducted in this careless fashion, what will be the result whenever there is a disturbance in any town ? Im-

mediately the troops will be requisitioned to keep the peace, and immediately that municipality will repudiate its obligation and oblige the government to pay the troops. That will be a serious condition of affairs. I say the law Is a good law, and ought to be administered and carried out in a way to compel these municipalities to pay their just debts. The Minister of Militia and Defence, or the Minister of Finance, or the Minister of Justice-because he is involved in it-somebody has to institute legal proceedings to recover this money, and the responsibility for doing so cannot be shifted on to the commanding officer of the militia. Somebody in the government is responsible, I think it is the Minister of Finance, and he ought not to rest until that money is returned.

My hon. friend, although like myself not a lawyer, knows something probably of the glorious uncertainties and the inglorious delays of the law. He knows that if an individual or a municipality wishes to repudiate its debts it can occupy a good deal of time. Now, I am correct in stating that there is a suit pending, and has been pending for some time against the municipality of Valleyfield for this money, that it is being pressed forward as rapidly as possible.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: When was the writ issued ?
I cannot say, but I will get the particulars.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I deemed it necessary on this item to bring the question to the notice of the government. I do not blame my hou. friend the Minister of Militia so much as the whole government collectively. Those who have any knowledge of what took place in 1900 in the town of Valleyfield know perfectly well that the organization which was supposed to be an organization of labour, but which was in reality a purely political organization, provoked a strike just on the eve of an election. In. some way or other through the instrumentality of some one of the same political faith as the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, the militia was called out at Valleyfield just before the election, and the whole blame of this was, through some instrumentality, laid upon my friend Mr. Bergeron, so that he lost his election in consequence of these manoeuvres. Now we find that the government comes down and pays for the calling out of the militia, the sum of $4,480 and there is no further question raised whatever until a by-election comes on, and then, when the by-election comes on and when the question of this organization by which Mr. Bergeron was defeated in 1900 is threshed out before the people, we find that ministers of the Crown-I do not say the hon. Minister of
Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick), although he appeared to me to be pretty well aware of what was going on ; it may have been the hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) because he came down there- ministers of the Crown came down and gave the electors of the town of Valleyfield the complete assurance that they would never be called upon to pay a cent of this largo sum which was employed as a political manoeuvre. Now, I leave that aside, but what I would ask is this : What is going to be the rule ? We know the law, but is the law going to be applied ? If it is going to be applied in that way I say we must reimburse the city of Toronto for the money that has been expended there, and that it is unfair that these men who have been doing duty in the city of Montreal should not have been paid in full. I know many of them have suffered from not being paid. I know that many of the officers have been disagreeably situated on that account. But, I go further and say that yon must apply that rule to the city of Montreal as well, and if there are $15,000 or $20,000 to be paid there, it should be paid by the government. All I want is that justice shall be done, that the same rule shall be applied to everybody and that the machinery of the Militia Act and the Department of Labour shall not be used in any way for political purposes. It is proper that we should bring this matter to the attention of the House and the country.

Mr. Chairman. I cannot allow the statements which have been made tonight to go uncontradicted. I took part in that election. I attended every .meeting at which any of the ministers were present, and I never heard one single member of the government give any assurance to the electors of Valleyfield that that amount would not be collected from them.
Hear, hear.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: There is another point which I think it well to contradict, and that is the statement in respect to the labour union being a political organization. If it was a political organization it was composed of both Conservatives and Liberals. There is also another statement that I wish to deny, and that is that the strike at Valleyfield was provoked by the labourers. In my own opinion, if an investigation were held, it would prove to the entire satisfaction of those who would be honest enough to admit proof, that it was the Montreal Cotton Company which was responsible for the strike of their employees.

My hon. friend (Mr. Loy) is giving himself a great deal of trouble contradicting what I did not say at all. Certainly, I am surprised that my hon. friend who has been some years in politics, should suppose that the ministers would go down to Valleyfield and state publicly that

they would give the town of Valleytield $4,480. . What I said was, and what I repeat is, that the statement was made by somebody in authority on the eve of the by-election and my hon. friend was elected.
Who made it ?

I did not attend the committee meetings or the private meetings where that assurance was made, but it was made and it had that effect. Nor did I say that the labourers of Valleyfield had provoked the strike. Why does the hon. gentleman take the trouble to contradict what I do not say ? The labourers of Valleyfield I know as well as my hon. friend does. I never treated them as my hon. friend treated them when he brought their affidavits into this House to read them, but what I say is that the organization which brought about that strike and called upon the mayor to call upon the troops, was conducting a political manoeuvre. We have proof of it to-day in the fact that the account has not been collected. The city of Toronto and the city of Montreal ought to stand in just as fair a position as Valley-field, yet Montreal and Toronto are treated in the way in which we know they are treated. This is the proper time to raise the question. Let the hon. minister give us an assurance that even justice will be dealt out to all before we vote this $391,000. It is only fair and I think we have a right to exact that.

I have no hesitation whatever in giving the assurance that we shall proceed under the law and that we will do our best. It is not always possible to do it, but we will do our best and see that even justice is given to all.
speakername: The MINISTER OE MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. and learned Minister of Justice when the writ was issued and who was the solicitor acting for the government in the endeavour to collect the money from the town of Valley-field ?

I am not aware that a writ issued nor am I aware that there has been a solicitor appointed to act for the government, because, as I read the statute, action must be taken by the commanding officer. He alone has the right to bring suit and he alone has control.

The hon. Minister of Justice knows perfectly well that although the commanding officer is the party who claims the amount, he is entirely under the control of the Department of Militia and Defence and of the government. At any rate I wish to make my own position clear in view of the statement of the hon. member for Beau-harnois (Mr. Loy). What I demand and what I think we have a right to exact from the government is that the same treatment should be meted out all around. I believe, as the hon. member for York (Mr. Maclean) Mr. MONK.
said, it might lead to grave abuses if this practice is adhered to, because, the hon. Minister of Justice will, himself, admit that abuses would be easy. Upon the slightest trouble of any kind whatever you could requisition the militia and cause considerable expense and profit to certain individuals and the municipality, being on the right side, probably, would have nothing to fear. I believe the law is a good one, but it has to be administered in the same way for all parties.
The hon. gentleman will see that it is the city authorities themselves who make a requisition for troops ; therefore, that seems to safeguard the question of improper expenditure.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Loy) has just told us that the militia were brought to Valleyfield on the requisition of the Montreal Cotton Company. Is that right ?
No, no.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman, ns I understand, said that.
No, that was not the fact any way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: He said that the strike was caused by the Montreal Cotton Company.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, then. But it all goes to show how necessary it is that we should understand where we are in this matter. If a strike is caused by a company whose head office is many miles away from the scene of the disturbance, and the local authorities are requested to bring the militia out for the purpose of awing the strikers, it should be clearly understood that the expenditure for the maintenance of these troops should be borne by the municipality. The gravest possible abuse may arise in the calling out of troops here or there where their services are not required. If the precedent is established in this ease, that for certain reasons a municipality must not bear the responsibility of its action in calling out troops, then other municipalities may call out troops when their services are not required. It would be scandalous if one rule is applied to Valleyfield, and another to Montreal, and another to Toronto. We are entitled to know what action the government purposes taking to spur on the commanding officer of that regiment to do his duty. It appears to be one of those cases where it is nobody's business to act. The militia were entitled to be paid for their services, and the government having disbursed $4,000 or $5,000 of the money of the people, they should take steps to collect that money from ' the municipality if the law says the muni-

cipality is responsible. Will tlie Minister of Militia tell us whether he will give the proper officer instructions to proceed forthwith to collect this money from the municipality of Valleyfield ?
The MINISTER OF - MILITIA AND DEFENCE. It is not a case of the minister giving instructions, but I certainly shall inquire to ascertain why this officer has not done his duty, and then it will be my business to deal with the officer.

Quite so. If it is the duty of the officer to protect the public treasury as well as life and property, and if it is his duty to collect the money from the municipality, surely he is guilty of a gross dereliction of his duty if he does not proceed forthwith.
I think so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Will the minister take cognizance of that ?
Certainly I will.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The Minister of Justice evades his responsibility anti the responsibility of the government who profess to be the watch dogs of the treasury by casting the blame upon some officer. I, for one, am not willing that this question should pass until there is an assurance from the Minister of Finance that he considers it his duty to recover that money at the earliest possible moment. We have been told that irregularities in connection with the Militia Department are to-day the subject of inquiry by special commission. Here is work for another special commission. I don't know that I have ever heard before that money can be paid out of the treasury without warrant, and that no steps are to be taken to recover it from the municipality which owes it. I will not be satisfied until 1 have a statement from the Minister of Finance that as guardian of the treasury, and as the custodian of the people's money, he Intends to get that money back. It is nice to see the Minister of Justice laugh at the idea of the government being custodians of the money of the people. It is a joke. Open the bag boys and pass the money around ; that's their idea of it. The men who have the public money to guard, occupy a sacred trust, but these gentlemen on the treasury benches do not seem to understand that. I want an assurance that the Minister of Finance does intend to get that money back, that the Minister of Justice will assist him in getting it back, and that the Minister of Militia will insist on the commanding officer doing his duty in the premises.

I certainly would not have spoken again were it not for the nttempt by the government to fasten the
responsibility upon the commanding officer, and I am surprised that the Minister of Militia should allow such a thing to be done. As soon as the men are paid, the commanding officer has no further interest except that the law says his name shall be used in an action for the recovery of the money. If the Minister of Militia is going to hold the commanding officer responsible for the collection of this debt, I am satisfied that every militia officer in the country will resent such a thing, and that not one of them would serve an hour longer. It is absurd to contend that a commanding officer should be put to the expense and risk of entering a suit to recover such money for the Crown. If that is the iaw then there is not one officer out of ten who would take such a responsibility. For my part, I would not. Does any one mean to say that the Minister of Militia is going to stand up here in the face of the militia of Canada and say that this officer is neglecting his duty. Why the thing is absurd. I would resign my position as Minister of Militia, much as I might pride in it, before I would allow such a principle to be laid down. The Minister of Justice cannot disclaim his responsibility. When I was Minister of Militia, if such a thing occurred, instructions would have been sent to the Justice Department to collect the money, and then the responsibility would be upon the Minister of Justice. If the Minister of Justice received such instructions he is responsible, and he is doubly responsible as a member of the cabinet, because the whole cabinet is responsible in a sense for the proper administration of any one department. It is absurd to say that it is the duty of the commanding officer to move without the initiative of the Minister of Militia, and then the action should be taken on the responsibility of the Minister of Justice. I do not believe that on consideration, the Minister of Militia will take the responsibility of saying that the commanding officer in this case is in any way responsible for the neglect to collect this money. We are given to understand that it is the duty of the commanding officer to take action, but the Militia Department should be behind him, so that, even if he is in South Africa his name can be used. I agree with the hon. member for East York that the most important question is whether the responsibility is to be shifted from the department to the officer.

I think it well to state that so far as I know a demand was made on the town of Valleyfield for the payment of the expenses in connection with militia being called ouj:. I know that the town refuses to pay the whole amount demanded. I do not know whether it assumes the responsibility of part of it; but I think it does. I know that the demand was made on the town.
I Some hon. MEMBERS. By whom ?

By the Militia Department or by some one authorized by the government; but I think the town is resisting the claim, or a part of it. I think it is only right for me to say that, in respect to the charge which was made, that some one had been authorized to promise that the amount would not be collected. For my part, I assisted at nearly every meeting, and I do not know of any person being authorized to make any such statement. I would be glad if the hon. gentleman would give me the name of the party who made that statement.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if in his opinion this debt is going to be collected from the town of Aralleyfield, or if it is not, going to be collected 1
I may say, in reply to the hon. gentleman, that the town claims that it was not responsible, because the strike was provoked by the employees of the Montreal Cotton Company.
Will the hon. gentleman inform us at what date that demand was made ?
I cannot tell the date.

I would like to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Militia to a short discussion which took place on this item last session. On page 4260 of ' Hansard ' I lind the following :
Contingencies-further amount required, $4,500.

This is simply to reimburse the department for the amount paid over to the troops in connection with the Valleyfield riots. Proceedings were taken to collect that money from the town, but in the meantime the men had to be paid and were paid out of contingencies. There was no other way of paying them.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Prom whom are you trying to collect the money ?

From the town. From that it would appear that proceedings were taken at that time, and I think we should be told by whom those proceedings were taken, what was the result, and what is the reason for the delay since last session. I am sure the hon. minister will be able to give us that information.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I have no Information. I have no doubt that what I said at that time was absolutely true, and was said after 1 had made inquiry in the department. I did not expect that this question would be asked tonight, and I am not prepared with the dates: but I have no doubt whatever in my own mind that proceedings have been taken and are going on to recover that money, and we propose to recover it if it is possible to do so. My hon. friend from South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) did not quite apprehend my meaning when he assumed that I proposed to throw the whole responsibility upon Mr. LOY.
the commanding officer. What I said was that I would cause inquiry to be made to see why the officer had not performed the duty assigned to him under the statute. I said nothing about his responsibility, or about his paying the money out of his own pocket, or paying the cost of the suit, or anything of the kind. The statute prescribes a duty for the commanding officer to perform, and I said that I would inquire and ascertain why he had not performed his duty-that is all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I think the first thing to be done is to ascertain the fact before we proceed to pass judgment on what has occurred. The first tiling to be ascertained is whether or not the commanding officer has performed the duty assigned tet him by the statute. If he has, then it would be a matter of inquiry, I apprehend, to ascertain whether or not he has proceeded diligently or has been remiss in the performance of his duty. If he has not performed the duty assigned to him, then it seems to me that it is properly within the jurisdiction of the committee to inquire why he has not performed his duty. But let us start by knowing whether or not anything has been done. When we ascertain the fact, then we can apportion the blame and determine on the responsibility. I would like to make a statement of the law, as I understand it, with regard to the calling out of troops by the civil power. It is a matter of statutory duty. The government is absolutely without power to interfere, either to call out troops or to prevent them being called out. The very moment peace is disturbed within the limits of a municipality, those who represent the civil power in that municipality have a right under the statute to call on the military authorities for assistance, and it is the duty of the military I authorities to give those who represent the j civil power that measure of assistance which they think necessary. Up to that point the government cannot interfere in any way. When the civil authorities make their demand, they make it upon the senior officer in the district, who in the exercise of his discretion calls upon such number of the militia force as he thinks necessary under the circumstances to give to the civil authorities the measure of aid they require. In that he acts within his discretion. After he has performed his duty, and the services of the troops are no longer required, the question of remuneration comes up for consideration. It is then the duty of the commanding officer to apply to the civil authorities who are responsible for his action in the premises, to liquidate the obligations which he has contracted towards the militia. If there is any default or hesitation on their part, the statute provides that he can apply to the government. The funds are then taken out of the consolidated revenue fund for the purpose of liquidating this obligation to the militia; but that is only a temporary

expedient.* The duty still remains on the commanding officer in his own name to proceed against the municipality-I am reading from tiie statute-'for the recovery of such pay, allowances and cost of transport, and he shall, on receipt thereof, pay over the amount to Her Majesty.' Therefore, hou. gentlemen will see at a glance that the duty in the first instance is>
on the commanding officer. If he fails in his duty, then it is for the government to consider how far they can interfere, using his name, to force him to recover the amount, or to recover the , amount by direct action. The first thing is ' to ascertain whether or not he has performed his duty in the premises. That is a matter of inquiry, and the Minister of Militia will be in a position to inform the committee when his estimates come up tomorrow.

I understand that the question was put in the Senate to-day by the Hon. Senator Landry, whether judicial proceedings had been taken to recover from the town of Valleyfield the amount paid by the Militia Department for calling out" the troops, and what was the amount paid by the department ? To these questions the Hon. Mr. Scott replied that the amount paid was $4,480, and that a suit was pending for that amount.
Then I am out of it.

I do not think that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice will claim that it is now the duty of the government to study the question and find out whether it is possible to get this officer to urge his suit. No doubt this officer is performing a statutory duty under the direction of the government. I do not want to blame that officer, but I want equal rights, and I will put this last question to the Minister of Militia and Defence : Will he give us the assurance that he will not press this claim against the city of Montreal until he has settled the Valley-field business ? That affair is three years old, and if he will make this promise, I shall not criticise any further.
