The only assurance I can give is that the letter of the law will be applied in the case of Montreal as in every other case.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: As in the case of Valley-field ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
That may be very satisfactory for Valleyfield and Montreal, but I would like to know where Toronto comes in.
I think that we should have the assurance of the hon. minister that he will send a department cheque to the city of Toronto for the moneys that city contributed to pay for the calling out of the militia. If Valleyfield and Montreal are to go scot free. Toronto should be reimbursed.

I am afraid I have not the power.
_ Mr. KEMP. The hon. Minister of Justice, in the graphic way in which he has explained the mode of procedure, seems to throw the responsibility on the commanding officer. But to my mind the commanding officer is simply a figure head. Who has to supply him with the sinews of war to carry on a lawsuit, if it be not the department ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: It is not I who am throwing the responsibility on the commanding officer, but it is the statute which puts the responsibility both on the government and on him. The statute puts the responsibility on the government of paying. in case of default by the municipality, and then puts the responsibility on the commanding officer of collecting the money, just as absolutely as it puts upon him the responsibility of calling out the troops when requisitioned to do so by the civil authorities. With regard to legal expenses, there has never been any request made to the government to come to the assistance of the commanding officer under the circumstances. When he seeks to collect the amount due, under the conditions described, the expenses are very trivial, and I have never known a commanding officer to apply to the government for aid, but if he did his request would be favourably considered.
It is not in the usual order of things that a lawsuit for $4,000 er $5,000 can be carried on two or three years without involving heavy costs.
This case is not without a precedent. My hon. friends from Quebec will not forget the case that occurred at Pontiac in 1895.
That was under another government.

In this case it is quite clear that if the commanding officer has not done his duty and does not wish to do it, there must be some means by which we can recover from the municipality the amount we have paid to liquidate an obligation it is under to the militia.
Would it be possible for the commanding officer to issue a writ without the knowledge of the Minister of Justice ?
Yes, he would retain his own counsel without any reference to the department.
Is there any correspondence respecting the issue of a writ ?

I could not possibly answer now. There is a lot of work done in the department without my

personal knowledge. I shall let my hon. friend know everything we have in the department.
Will the hon. minister give us the correspondence regarding the payment of the militia at Valleyfield ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I suppose the same delay will be given Montreal as the town of Valleyfield ?

We will ask Montreal to pay as promptly as Toronto did.
Annual drill and musketry, $520,000.
What is the number you propose to drill ?

Last year the report indicates that the system of what is called skeleton drill was adopted, and the camps were composed very largely of officers, non-commissioned officers and a very few men. This year'it is proposed to send more men, but still to continue the skeleton drill, which the general officer commanding seems to think works very well. The best selected men from the different companies will be taken into camp, about twenty-two men for each company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I wish to ask if any provision will be made this year for increased pay to the men ? The hon. minister knows how difficult it is to procure men under existing conditions. I would be glad to know if. should the Bill he brought down this session, or by any other way, provision will be made for increased pay.

I may say to my hon. friend that even if the BUI should be brought down this session there would be no provision in it with regard to pay. It is not proposed to include in the new Bill a scale of pay as is done in the present law. That would be left to the executive and to parliament to settle from year to year. I hope, however, that a solution of the difficulty may he reached in this way. Beginning at fifty cents for the first year, for every additional year that a man serves, up to say five years, there should be given good conduct additions of five or ten cents, as is done in the North-west Mounted Police. We have not actually adopted that scheme, but it was recommended by the former general officer commanding, and I think the present general is in favour of it. And I must say that it appeals to me as being one of the best ways, perhaps the most effective way, in which we could deal with this question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I understand, then, that this is purely an estimate, that it is not based on actual numbers ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I understand that neither numbers nor rates of pay have been settled. I see the men are ordered out in June
The rate of pay will be the same as last year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Will the other questions be dealt with in the supplementary estimates ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: And information will then be given and we shall be free to discuss-
Absolutely.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: But this is not intended to cover that-it will be in the sup-plimentary estimates ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Does the hon. minister intend to hold a camp at Niagara this year ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: When I was at home last week, they told me they had received no word about it.
There is to be a camp.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: In June ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I would urge upon the government, in view of what the hon. minister has said, the necessity of increasing the pay to the young men who go out to the camps. There are a number of very fit young men who should be in the camp at Niagara, but, it would be altogether too much to expect them to go out for .fifty cents a day. The commanding officers tell me that it is almost impossible to get them, that it is asking too much of the young men. when they are so busy with their fruitgrowing and other things-the very best class of young men, well fit for drill and willing to go, but quite unable to leave their duties at that time unless fairly paid. So, if the hon. minister has not determined the rate of pay he is going to give these young men, I would urge him to materially increase it. Considering the way things are going now and the rates of pay men are receivingworking at! other things than learning drill in order to serve their country, these young men should be paid considerably more than is paid now.

It is as well, perhaps, to say a word or two on that point. There is a great deal in what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) says. But the hon. gentleman will see that if we undertake to pay a man what you might call adequate, reasonable fair wages, we would at once practically double the militia vote-more than double it. Well, now, I really don't think that is necessary. Much as I would like to increase the pay, I think we have a right to expect now and in the future what we have had in the past- a response to this demand for military service on the part of young men who have a taste for it and are willing and anxious to undertake it if they are only indemnified for actual money loss. I believe that a very large percentage of the young men who turn out do not go for the money. Otherwise, at this moment, it would be very difficult to get men to go into camp no matter what you might do, because they are so busy with their own personal affairs. It would take a very large sum of money to tempt them if it were not for this love of the service, this strong military ardour. I do not think it is largely a question of money at all. I believe that we shall get the men as we have done in the past. Forty years ago when I first joined the militia of my own province, no such thing as pay was talked about, and we had in the province of Nova Scotia as large a militia as we have now in the whole Dominion of Canada. The men turned out without a dollar- turned ' out because they liked it and because they felt it to be a duty. I do not think that we should hold out to the young men of this country the expectation that this parliament is going to vote them any very large sum of money. Rather I would expect them to do, as I said a moment ago, now and in the future, what has been done by our young men hitherto, that is, give their services, provided the government indemnifies them for actual loss of money. I think that we should give them more than we do now. But I do not think there should be a very material increase.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The hon. minister, perhaps, has not understood me. I did not wish to say on behalf of these young men that they want to make money out of their military service. There are two extremes to this matter, and perhaps we are at one extreme to-day. What I mean is that at the present rate of pay they are not indemnified for actual loss, and would not be at three times the amount. What I submit is that there ought to be a better average struck. There is no lack of military ardour, but the fact remains that these young men are simply unahle to pay their debts and give their time to this military service for so small a sum as fifty cents a day. They do not ask to be even fully indemnified, but they do ask to be better indemnified than they are now, and I think they should be.
That is a fair question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I confess that I am somewhat disappointed by what the hon. minister has said with regard to the paying. I doubt, even if the pay were increased by the small ratio the minister suggests, that it would be satisfactory. I wish to call the mjnistjer's attention to one thing which militates against the regiment which I have the honour to command in securing men. There are two other arms of the service in the county from which my regiment is recruited, the artillery and the cavalry, find each is allowed a dollar a day for a horse. That is, a horse is counted to be worth double what a man is. When these young farmers can get $1.50 a day by taking a horse, they much prefer the arms of the service that offer that opportunity. I think, notwithstanding what the minister says about patriotism and all that sort of thing, that the men who give their services to the country for these twelve days in the year are entitled to a better treatment from the government than they receive. It seems to me that, when only half the number of men of each company are to be taken out, a small advance might be given in the pay of those who are going to serve. I would strongly urge upon the minister to reconsider this matter and, if possible, to consider it in the light of the increase of the facilities the country has for obtaining money. It seems to me that when the revenue is so large, the militia should obtain a little benefit from it. I trust he will give his consideration to the case, and I am sure it would be greatly to the benefit of the militia if he would do so.
Will the minister tell us /at what time in June the camp will assemble in Niagara ?
I think it is the 23rd, but I am not absolutely certain.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: It is the 9th, I believe.
No, I think it is later than the 9th. There is a camp on the 9th at Dese-ronto.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: At Niagara.
Then the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) is right. It has all been published in the newspapers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I was discussing it the other day; I feel safe in saying that it is the 9th.

There also was to have been a camp in Kingston on the 16th. I would like to ask why that has been changed to the 23rd ? It is a less convenient date, be-

cause the troops are kept in camp on a holiday, the 1st of July, which they would prefer to spend at home. If the camp at Kingston could be arranged for the 16th, the men would arrive home before the 1st of July. I am sure, however, it would be much more satisfactory if the camp were held on the 16th.

All I can say is that it is a detail, as my hon. friend from South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) will appreciate, which the military branch control and settle, and they do it after corresponding with the district officers commanding in the different districts. I do not interfere in the slightest respect, but since the matter has been mentioned, I will have great pleasure in bringing my hon. friend's observations to the notice of the Adjutant General.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Is there going to be a camp v at Laprairie this year ?	.
I believe not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What is the reason the department has ceased to have a camp at Laprairie ? I think it has been now some time since we have had a camp at Laprairie.

Two years, I think. The reason the camp was not held at Laprairie two years ago was because of an outbreak of small-pox. It became necessary to secure another camping ground, and a very favourable place was found at Three Rivers, and at a reasonable cost. A camp was held there last year, and I believe will be held there this year. The General Officer Commanding was very much pleased with it, and he again selected the place for a camp this year. The hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Monet) has spoken to me with reference to this very matter, and I assured him that very likely next year a general camp would be again held at Laprairie. There is only one camp being held in the whole province of Quebec, at Three Rivers, which is the most convenient place, and the cost of transportation is somewhat less at that point. It is more central than Laprairie. Nevertheless, the Laprairie camp was a very good one. I think it is desirable that these camps should be changed from time to time. The whole militia of the province of Quebec camped at Laprairie three or four years ago, and there is no reason why it should not do so again.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Had the member for Laprairie made these representations before the minister had determined upon Three Rivers for the camp this year ? Is there any correspondence ?
No, I think not. He spoke to me about it only to-day.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Is it the intention to have the camp at Laprairie next year ?

It is probable. I may explain that these are matters which are settled chiefly by the staff here, the General Officer Commanding and the Adjutant General, witli the officers he has around him, with the assistance of the officers commanding the different districts. I never interfere with recommendations of this kind that are sent to me, because I think these gentlemen know the most about it. Still, I do know that Laprairie is a good ground, and I think it probable that the General Officer Commanding will recommend that a camp be held there, perhaps next year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: "Small-pox is the reason why the camp was not held there two years ago?

Yes. There was no reason why we did not go there last year except that we had a good ground at Three Rivers.
Salaries and wages, $95,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I want to ask the committee to allow me to divide this item. The money provided here is for the purpose of paying the stores branch of the department, and also for the care of buildings, rifle ranges, &c. It is intended on the 1st of July to place the stores in the military branch under the supervision of the General Officer Commanding. That has been decided upon since the estimates have been made up, therefore, I want to transfer out of this vote $45,000 to the vote for pay and allowances.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What distinction do you draw ? This covers salaries, wages, superintendents of stores, inspectors of clothing and miscellaneous employees. Are you going to take miscellaneous employees out and leave the stores alone ?

The hon. gentleman knows that we have a chief superintendent of stores at Ottawa, who has a considerable number of officers and clerks under him. He also has a stores branch and a superintendent of stores in every military district in the Dominion. Now it is proposed to create a department of ordnance, with the chief superintendent of stores as a military officer at the head of that department. He will be called the director-general of ordnance, and his department will then become military, and will be paid out of the fund for pay and allowances. I wish to transfer that portion of this vote, and to carry to the officers and men of the stores branch to the pay and allowance vote, so that they can be paid from that vote instead of as in the past.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: It will take all the employees of the stores into the military branch.
Exactly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Is that change provided for in the new Bill ?
It is not necessary to provide for it by statute. The present law is sufficient.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I forgot to ask the minister whether we will have that Bill down before the supplementaries are taken up, because if we are going to have a general discussion then, we ought to have all the information.

Certainly. I intended to say to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), in reply to an observation he made, that I am prepared, when the general discussion is taken up, to state, and perhaps before that, what we intend to do with reference to introducing the Bill this year. I have given notice of the Bill, but there are some reasons why it has been impossible to go on with it. Now, Mr. Chairman, I move to transfer $45,000 of this vote to number 74. It will be a permanent change. This vote will be reduced to $50,000. It is a matter, perhaps, for the clerk to settle how it shall be done, but surely it would be possible to divide this vote into two parts, and to say ' pay and allowance, $45,000 in addition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Item 76 would then read as follows :
. That a sum not exceeding $436,405 be granted to His Majesty. &c.
That would be adding the $45,000 to the $391,405 for pay and allowances.
That is not the best way to do it.
No, I do not think so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Say in addition to pay and allowances $45,000, and then you would have the $50,000 for other purposes. I notice there is an addition in that vote of $5,000.

Yes, it is due largely to the additional number of caretakers. We are building armouries, drill halls and new rifle ranges, and the employees in connection with these will be paid out of this vote of $50,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Where are you appointing these new caretakers ?
The MINISTER OF MILITIA) AND DEFENCE. Take military district No. 11, for instance; there is an increase of $631 owing to the appointment of W. L. Davis, as caretaker, at a salary of $540. In district No. 9, which is in Nova Scotia, there is a clerk, Major Black, appointed at a salary of $540.
What is he required for ?

He does work for the district officer commanding. I may explain in regard to this officer that he was the brigade major when I came in, a very deserving man, but he was stricken with illness and rendered unfit to do that work. He is able, however, to do clerical work. He could not come under the pension law and as he was not very well provided with this world's goods it seemed a public duty that we should make some provision for him. Then, there is a man named F. R. Hiltz, who was employed as caretaker of an armoury at $1 a day, and John Potter who is employed at the armoury in Cumberland county, also receives $1 a day. That makes an increase of $1,277 there. So I might go through the whole list.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What I want to know is if these men are employed where new armouries have been provided, or are they additions to the staffs in localities which are already supplied ?
No, they are employed at new armouries.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I mean all through- the balance of the additions.
Yes, pretty much. There are some cases of increased wages. There are increases! from $1 to $1.25, and from $1.25 to $1.50 a day. .
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister if these soldiers who went; out to South Africa and who were in the employ of the government have all been taken back since they returned ?
So far as I know. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) will remember that a return was moved for and that return, I know, has been prepared by every department and will be laid on the Table of the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I wish to invite the hon. minister's attention to the case of a man named Herbert Cottee, who writes me from 257 Bolton street. As I understand his communication he was ten years in the service of the government. He went out with the 4th contingent, joined as a private, was promoted to be lance corporal and has not been taken back since his return.
What department was he in ?

He says :
I have been in the employ of the government for over ten years and was the only one to my knowledge that did not receive his position hack on returning from South Africa. Then, X know others who received full pay when absent

who volunteered when I did. I trust you will do what you can for me.
I remain, respectfully,
(Sgd.) HERBERT GOTTEE.
I really think the case of this man may have been overlooked.
The MINISTER OF MILITIA', AND DEFENCE. I will be very glad to look into it.

He is very deserving, I should judge from his communication, and perhaps, when we continue the discussion of these estimates, the hon. minister will have looked into the case and will see that justice is done to him.

If my hon. friend will send me the papers, I will give him an answer tomorrow. I may say though, that I think Mr. Cottee is mistaken in saying that in the last contingent in which he was, any officers were paid their salaries. I may be wrong. In the first and second contingents that was done, but latterly I do not think it was done, although I will not be absolutely positive.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: He may be mistaken as to that, but I think in other respects his claim may be worth looking into.
I will look into it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think it would be well that we should amend the phraseology of item 76 so as to read that:
A sum not exceeding $95,000 be granted to His Majesty for salaries, wages, pay and allowances.
That would leave it uncertain. It seems to me that we should divide it into two items.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It could be made to read in this way : ' Salaries and wages $50,000 ; making one item, and then another item saying : ' Pay and allowances $45,000.'

That will do.
Item as amended voted.
Military properties, $190,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
This is the usual vote. There is $35,000 for maintenance of drill halls, &c., and rentals and renewals of military properties generally ; rent of buildings and rifle ranges, $10,000; fuel for buildings and rifle ranges. $10,000 ; lighting, $12,000 ; water, $1,000; sundry expenses, $2,000. There is a certain amount required annually in the different districts for repairs and it is proposed to divide it in this way : London, $8,000; Toronto, $10,000; Kingston, $8,000; Montreal, $8,000; St. Johns, $5,000; Quebec, $10,000; Fredericton, $8,000; Halifax, $5,000; Winnipeg, $2,000; Victoria, $2,000; Charlottetown, $2,000, and Ottawa, Mr. MONK.
$5,000. For putting up armouries generally, $5,000. There is $20,000 to keep the historic walls of Quebec in some sort of respectable shape. We have been voting this money for the past three years, and they are in a much better condition than they were. There is $8,000 for general repairs for the cartridge factory; repairs to the Wolseley barracks, London, $5,000; repairs to Stanley barracks, $2,000; Toronto cavalry quarters, $1,500; extension of drill hall at Ottawa; Royal Military College, installation of Are protection; Quebec, heating officers' quarters, general repairs to store buildings, painting and general repairs to R.C.R.I. barracks; general repairs at Levis; levelling grounds for Bedford rifle ranges, $5,000; new sidewalks around drill hall, Halifax, $2,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Last year the same sum of $190,000 was voted for this purpose, but it would appear from the Auditor General's Report that $268,000 was spent. What is the explanation of that. There was.$315,-000 spent for the annual camps out of a vote of $520,000. Would the excess expenditure on one vote come out of the balance left from the other.
It ought not to. I cannot give the information now, but I will make a'note of it and give the explanation later.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I see that there was an under expenditure of about $23,000 for pay and allowances last year.
That happens almost every year in connection with that vote.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: There is a statement as to the lapsed amounts in the Auditor General's Report, but that item does not appear amongst them. For annual drill and musketry there was $520,000 voted last year and only $314,000 expended. However, the minister says he will get the explanation.
That item includes stores and equipment of all kinds and last year we added considerably to the equipment and stores and the balance of the vote was expended in that way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: It does not seem as if any of these repairs at any place have been done by contract. That is very regrettable. The citadel of Quebec seems to have been stormed every day since the celebrated battle of the Plains of Abraham. Twelve thousand dollars of work seems to have been done by the day. _
I think it would be impossible to do that work by contract. I am so advised.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I am afraid the minister has got among very bad people in my own province; it makes me feel doubly sorry to say

so. None of these repairs amounting to over $5,000 seem to have been done by contract. This naturally excites some curiosity. What are the repairs to the citadel to the amount of $20,000 to be done this year ?
The MINISTER! OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE. If the hon. gentleman will look at the Militia report, at page 22, he will find all the details.

I think it is sufficient to look at the public accounts of last year to see that a great saving would be effected by giving most of these things out by contract. The plumbers seem to have held an orgy last year, and if we pursued the rule we would have more money for the militia.

All new plumbing work is given out by tender, and I assure the hon. gentleman that wherever possible we ask for tenders; but for such work as repairing these old walls it is impossible to get tenders, and I think it is in the public interest to pursue the course we have been pursuing in that respect.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister if there is any truth in the report which reaches us from time to time to the effect that the government intend to establish a new military depot in the city of Montreal ? I believe that the establishment of such a depot would be productive of much good, and, as the hon. gentleman is aware, deputations have come to Ottawa several times in connection therewith. We have no small-pox there at present. I mention that because I see the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Monet) here, for I believe the camp lias been taken away from there because of small-pox. But we have none in Montreal, and we would be glad to have a military depot there.
I cannot make any positive announcement now; but if the hon. gentleman will carefully scan the supplementary estimates, he may be pleased with what he will see there.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has alluded to the small-pox at Laprairie, as having caused the removal of the camp from there to Three Rivers a few years ago. But I am glad to know that next year we may have the camp at Laprairie again.
That was the explanation of the camp being taken away in the first year, but it did not apply the second year.
There was still some smallpox there.
I am afraid that my hon. friend seeks an excuse, that is not to be found in disease, except another kind of disease.
There were two or three eases there.
The hon. gentleman has assumed too much from what the minister said, in saying that the camp will be brought back to Laprairie next year.
I said I hoped it would.

I would like to know whether any provision has been made by the Militia Department or the Public Works Department for completing the work on the Toronto drill shed. I feel it incumbent upon me to bring the matter to the attention of the minister. I have already on several occasions, as the minister is aware, brought it to his attention and also to the attention of the Minister of Public Works. It is after all a serious matter, in which both this government and the previous government are involved, and it should be disposed of in one way or the other. As the minister knows, we have three or four fine corps in Toronto. I believe he has authorized additions to the cavalry corps, and, in view of this fact, it is the duty of his department or the Department of Public Works to take the necessary steps to complete this work. Three or four years ago this matter was brought up formally by the city of Toronto. A resolution was adopted in 1899, setting forth the conditions under which the drill shed site was granted, and calling on the hon. Minister of Militia to proceed witli the erection of the armouries for the cavalry and artillery, as shown by the government plans and as formerly intended. The matter has been discussed recently, as the hon. minister is aware. I believe His Worship the Mayor of Toronto brought the matter to the attention of the government when he was down here a short time ago, and there has been some correspondence published recently in the newspaper press respecting the conditions under which the city of Toronto provided the $150,000 for the site. There were two letters respecting this matter published in the Toronto ' News ' of Saturday, the 9th of May-one from Col. George T. Denison, the other from Col. .T. H. Mead. Col. Denison has been for a life-time connected with the militia. He was formerly commander of the Governor General's bodyguard, and was very active at the time steps were being taken to procure the passage of the money by-law for purchasing the site. Col. Denison is a reputable citizen and a militia officer of very high standing, and I shall take the liberty of reading his letter because I cannot put in stronger language the obligation which I conceive to be binding on the government of completing the work whieh the government pledged itself to perform when the citizens voted $150,000, and purchased the site.
Heydon Villa, Toronto, October 1, 1902.
My dear Howland,-You were asking me about the understanding as to building the cavalry quarters as well as the artillery quarters along

with the armouries. I remember well the circumstances. The plan prepared by the government and shown to the officers commanding corps included accommodations for the infantry. cavalry and artillery. It was all one proposition, one building really and for the whole fores, and we were told and we informed our men and our friends that if we could get the by-law passed and the money voted for the purchase of the land that the building would be built by the government. We all worked for the by-law and voted for it, and have paid our share of the taxes for the land upon that understanding. When the land was got, a portion only of the building was put up-the infantry were provided for and the cavalry and artillery done out of theirs.
I have been enforcing criminal law for twenty-five years, and have sent down hundreds of criminals to the penitentiary or Central prison for fraud and obtaining money under false pretenses, and the moral wrong has often been no worse than the wrong done to the cavalry and artillery, whose taxes have been paid for years to buy land upon the false ^pretense that they would get certain specific rooms and quarters.
Yours very truly,

That is a pretty strong indictment to make against the government of Canada. I happened to he the chief executive officer of the city at the time this bylaw was voted, and I know that had it not been for the active co-operation of the officers and men of the militia in the city of Toronto, the citizens would not have voted the sum of $150,000 to purchase this site. They had the assurance of the Minister of Militia that if the money were voted, the required building would be furnished by the government. The citizens, in good faith, voted the money and purchased the site-a magnificent site in the heart of the city. The militia force of Toronto are cramped for accommodation, as the Minister of Militia well knows. The Department of Public Works and. the Militia Department are in duty bound to keep their part of the bargain. There was an understanding that if the citizens of Toronto would purchase the site, the government would put up a building to accommodate the various branches of the service, and it is only fair that the government should keep faith and provide accommodations for the artillery and cavalry. There is also a letter from Colonel Mead. Colonel Denison was the commanding officer of the cavalry, the Governor General's Body Guard, and Colonel Mead was the officer commanding the Toronto Field Battery. Colonel Mead wrote as follows
Toronto, October 3, 1902. To His Worship the Mayor, Toronto.
Sir,-I have the honour to inform you that I was in command of the Toronto Field Battery of Artillery at the time negotiations were in progress between the government of Canada and the city of Toronto, respecting armouries for the accommodation of the militia force of this city. A plan was prepared by the government, showing accommodation proposed. This comprised a drill shed for the infantry, and a riding school for the mounted corps. In this Mr. CLARKE.
latter building, there was a satisfactory number of rooms for armouries, and squadron rooms for the cavalry, a gun shed and rooms also for the artillery.
I believed the plan submitted formed part of the agreement between the city and the government, and under this belief and as the riding school contained adequate accommodation for my corps, I approved of it. Similar approval having been obtained from the other officers commanding corps, the land was purchased by the city and, as I understood and believed, the government undertook to complete the two necessary buildings to accommodate the mounted corps of the city.
I constantly urged the completion of the arrangement, as ever since the construction of the one building for the infantry, the artillery has suffered greatly from want of adequate accommodation.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Yours very faithfully,
(Sgd.) J. H. MEAD,
Major-Lt.-Col.
I cannot put tbls case any stronger than the gentlemen whose letters I have read, have put it to the public and the government. It is a notorious fact that the militia has not sufficient accommodations for its stores. It is also notorious that two or three years ago the officer commanding the district, Colonel Otter, made application to the city of Toronto for the use of a portion of St. Andrew's market buildings for the storing of certain material. Two years ago Colonel Otter wrote to the chairman of the property committee of the city hall in Toronto, and I shall put this letter on record again, in the hope that it may have some effect on the Ministers of Militia and Public Works. Colonel Otter, commanding district No. 2, wrote as follows :
Stanley Barracks,
Toronto. March 22, 1901.
Sir,-I have the honour to make application on behalf of a portion of the local militia force for the temporary use of the ' Arcade,' St. Andrew's market, for the purpose of storing guns, wagons and harness.
With the present strength of the city corps, it Is impossible to find enough accommodation in the armouries, and pending the provision of such, I am compelled to appeal to the municipal authorities, as no place adapted for the purpose In view can be obtained.
I sincerely trust your committee will see its way to recommending my application to the council, and that a favourable answer may be granted.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
-	W, D. OTTER, Col.,
C'omd'g M. D. No. 2.
The Chairman of the
Property Committee,
City Hall, Toronto.
Tbe committee, upon receipt of this letter, made tbe following report to tbe council : Temporary Use of Arcade in St. Andrew's Market for Storing Guns, &c.
Application has been made to your committee by Col. Otter, commanding M.D. No. 2, on behalf of the local militia force, for the temporary use of the Arcade in St. Andrew's market for the

purpose of storing guns, wagons and harness. In his communication. Col. Otter states that with the present strength of the city corps it is impossible to find enough accommodation in the armouries, and pending the provision of such he is compelled to appeal to the municipal authorities, as no place adapted for the purpose in view can be obtained.
Your committee, after due consideration, beg to recommend that the temporary use of the Arcade in the St. Andrew's Market be granted to the local Militia force for the purpose indicated, the council reserving the right to terminate this arrangement upon giving one month's notice to "Col. Otter, or to such officer as may be authorized to carry out the duties now performed by him.
Two years have elapsed since the council of the city of Toronto provided the additional accommodation necessary for the storage of this military equipment, and nothing has been done, although repeated demands have been made on the government, to provide the requisite accommodation. I telegraphed to-day to the City Clerk of Toronto to ascertain if the military authorities were still using St. Andrew's market for storage, and I have his reply : ' Yes, two rooms in market annex for storage.' This reply was sent by Mr. Littlejohn, City Clerk. Surely we have the right to ask the government to put up the necessary buildings and afford the accommodation required for the Toronto militia on the site which the people of Toronto have furnished out of their own pockets. Surely if one of the parties has lived up to its contract, the other is in duty bound to do so. We are not asking a favour, we are demanding a simple right. We are very proud of our militia. Many of them made considerable sacrifices to keep up their corps, and the government should treat them reasonably and fairly by fulfilling its pledge and keeping faith with men who are doing so much, as these young men are doing, in connection with the militia corps in Toronto to maintain the esprit de corps of the militia force.
X think we have the right to demand-I do it most respectfully, but as firmly as I can- that faith should be kept with the city of Toronto. I myself had something to do with getting that money voted. I had to carry out the work of getting that site expropriated, and I feel a good deal on this matter personally. We have fulfilled our part of the arrangement and provided a site at a cost of $150,000, that our militia forces might be provided with the accommodation necessary to make them reasonably comfortable. I have had sent to me clippings from the ' Globe,' the ' Mail ' and other newspapers, with respect to the accommodation provided at Buffalo, Malone and other places in New York State for the local militia companies, and they certainly put us to the blush. The accommodations in Buffalo armoury for one regiment are greater than the accommodations in the Toronto armoury for three or four. I hope it will not be necessary to bring this matter up any more.
I think we are not asking anything unreasonable when we ask to have this shed completed at once ; and I would appeal-and I do appeal with a good deal of confidence- to the present Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) and the present Minister of Militia and Defence (Hon. Sir Fred- . erick Borden) that this be disposed of, and that accommodation for the cavalry and artillery be provided at the earliest moment.
My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) says that there is nothing unreasonable in his asking that additional accommodation be given to the people of Toronto
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The militia.

For the militia. There is certainly nothing unreasonable in it. It is the hon. gentleman's duty to do so, and I am bound to say that he has performed that duty very faithfully. But my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) will not complain, I think, if I tell him that I do think it is not reasonable for him to hold my hon. colleague the Minister of Public Works and myself responsible for the failure of his own friends to fulfill their obligations. Now, I have always looked upon my hon. friend as one of the fairest, straightest men in this House or any other House. But I do think he might have said to this committee, when he is putting ail this on record in ' Hansard,' that the indictment which he read, penned by Colonel Denison, was an indictment against the late administration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: All the worse for the late administration. And all the more creditable to the hon. gentleman, if the late administration was derelict in its duty, that he should perform the work which it failed to perform.

This is a legacy which has come to us from the late administration. But, notwithstanding the letter that Colonel Denison has written, let me, to some extent, come to the rescue of my hon. friends, and let me tell him that I have diligently searched for one particle of evidence to show that there was any written understanding-and surely the business men of Toronto would not enter into an agreement to purchase $150,000 worth of land upon an agreement with the government without having it in writing-not a particle of writing that I have been able to find, not a single plan, or letter, or statement, or agreement of any kind or description, to show that the government of that day bound itself to do anything in particular with reference to the drill hall of Toronto. There is, apparently, an opinion abroad among the military people there that certain promises were made, but the plan to which my hon. friend has referred,
I have never been able to procure, though I have asked for it. But let me dismiss that



view of the case. I have agreed with my hon. friend on this floor before, and I agree with him now, that there should be increased accommodation given to the garrison of militia in the city of Toronto. Moreover, I do not care what the agreement was with the late government, or whether they kept their agreement or not, it is absolutely a fact, and I admit it, that the city of Toronto to-day requires a very considerable amount of increased accommodation for the militia of that city. I agree with all that my hon. friend has said as to the excellent character of the militia of the city of Toronto. In the time of trouble we would look to that city almost before any other place to respond to the call, if it were necessary to call the militia to arms ; and they would turn out and would do their duty as they have done their duty. Now, let me say a word as to the concrete question. I have made a recommendation to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, which he has now before him, and I sincerely hope that we shall be able to make provision for the additional accommodation which is greatly needed, which has been too long needed, in the city of Toronto.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I was very careful to say, in speaking of this matter that it was the government of Canada that was responsible. I did not attempt to throw the responsibility upon the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) or his colleagues. Since I have had the honour of a seat in this House I have not hesitated to draw attention to the laches of somebody in connection with this matter. The fact that the site was selected and approved of by the Department of Militia and the fact that only half of that site is occupied with a building, is evidence that the intention was to erect a further building to afford the necessary accommodation for the various branches of the service. The land that was expropriated was exceedingly expensive land. The city of Toronto would not expropriate a site double the extent of the present building if the citizens had not what they deemed to be a reasonably satisfactory assurance from the militia authorities that that land would be required and the necessary buildings erected. The construction of the present building was not completed until about the time when the late government left office. The same representations would have been made to them that are being made to hon. gentlemen opposite, had they remained in office. I do not know whether those representations would have been more successful, but certainly we could not have been much worse off than we are at the present time. The late government, whatever its faults, certainly carried out part of its contract with the city, for it erected the present splendid shed, and representations were being made to the iate government to complete that work. Governments, apparently, are very slow to move in matters

of this kind. I do not desire, Mr. Chairman, in bringing this matter up, either to remove responsibility from the late government in the first place or to throw any undeserved responsibility on the present government. But the Minister of Militia admits the fact that there is nothing like sufficient accommodation for the militia of the city of Toronto. The hon. gentleman, in his administration of the department, has increased the cava b y corps. There is, therefore, greater need for additional accommodation. I think I am justified in calling attention to this matter. And, if the hon. minister thinks that he will be relieved in any way by throwing the responsibility on his predecessors for not completing the building in one or two years, I am not at all concerned about that; I am satisfied that he should do that, provided he will do what I think he admits is reasonably and fairly his duty in the premises by insisting that the building intended to be put upon the site shall be completed and that our various regiments shall have the-space and accommodation they ask for and absolutely require.

I did not understand the Minister of Militia as answering the question put by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) about the establishment of new divisions of the permanent coips. The rumour is that there are to be three. I would be glad if the hon. minister would tell us whether that is true, and where these new companies are to be situated.

It is rather anticipating matters, but I may say that there will be a small addition to the permanent force. Just where the additions will be located lam not in a position to say because it has not been finally settled, and I do not think it would be proper to speak on the subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I would like to ask the Minister of Militia and Defence on what grounds the department charged the city of Montreal for calling out the militia ? This matter has been discussed in the city council of Montreal, and as I am also a member of the city council, I would like to get that information.

My hon. friend, I suppose, did not hear the discussion that has taken place this evening. It was pointed out that under the Statute the government had no direct responsibility in the matter at all. The Minister of Justice pointed out with great clearness that if a riot is threatened the mayor of the city may call upon the commanding officer of the militia in that district to turn out the militia to assist the civil authority. The law further provides that the municipality shall pay the militia, and that in the event of its not doing so, the government may take the money out of the consolidated revenue to pay the troops, and the commanding officer who called out the
3G21

troops shall immediately proceed to collect the money from the corporation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: But I want to point out to the minister that the property which was threatened belongs to the government, the city of Montreal cannot collect five cents in taxes upon it, and has nothing to do with it. We wanted to tax some sheds there recently, and took the case down to Quebec, and it was decided against the city. Why should not the government protect their own property now the same as in years gone by ?

Perhaps my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Anne, (Mr. Gallery) was not here when we had an assurance from the government that the city of Montreal would not be called upon to pay. I understood the Minister of Militia to say clearly that he would only call upon the city of Montreal to pay after Valleyfield had settled. My hon. friend knows, therefore, there is no danger of Montreal being called upon.

As a matter of fact, I said nothing of the kind. I want to say this, however, to my hon. friend, that it does not matter to whom the property belongs when a riot is threatened, whether it belongs to the Dominion government, or the provincial government, or the city. The corporation of Montreal is bound to see that order is maintained within its borders, and the law provides how that may be done and at whose expense.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Before we leave this item, I desire to call the attention of the minister to a peculiar item that I And in the Auditor General's Report, page Q-44. It is an item in connection with the expenditures on military properties, and is very peculiar. I find some gentlemen named Cote Freres did some work repairing walls, and they received 8370.98 for supervision. You would imagine that having received that much they would have sharpened their own tools. But I find here an item for sharpening and repairing 728 dozen of tools at fifteen cents a piece. That is 8,720 tools at fifteen cents a piece, $130. It seems to me out of all proportion for the work done, and I hope the minister will make an inquiry and find out what these tools were.

I give it up, but I will make an inquiry.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of the Minister of Militia and Defence, House adjourned at 12 o'clock, a.m., Wednesday.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.
